messages.subject: Re: Dynamic allocation array
messages.subject_clean: Dynamic allocation array
messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, April 1, 2015 at 11:00:07 AM UTC-4, Giorgio Paulon wrote:
> Hello!
>
> I'm trying to implement a function in the functions block in STAN. However, I do not know if I can allocate dynamically a vector. To be more precise, let us say I want to build a function that returns an array of matrices whose length is variable (but known, denoted by T for each user i).
>
> functions {
>
>   matrix[s,s] Q_mat[T[i]](int i,int s,vector[s*s-s] mu,matrix[k,s*s-s] beta,int T_in[n],int T[n]) {
>
>     /*
>     Calculation here...
>     */
>
>     return Q_mat;
>   }
>
> }
>
> However, the result from parser is:
>
> Error in stanc(file = file, model_code = model_code, model_name = model_name,  :
>   failed to parse Stan model 'model3D' with error message:
> SYNTAX ERROR, MESSAGE(S) FROM PARSER:
>
> ERROR at line 5
>   3:    functions {
>   4:
>   5:      matrix[s,s] Q_mat[T[i]](int i,int s,vector[s*s-s] mu,matrix[k,s*s-s] beta,int T_in[n],int T[n]) {
>                 ^
>   6:
>
> What am I doing wrong?
>
> Thank you very much in advance

User defined function declarations do not input (or check) the sizes of input or output. Write it like

functions {

  matrix[] Q_mat(int i,int s, vector mu, matrix beta, int[] T_in ,int[] T) {

   /*
   Calculation here...
   */
    return Q_mat;
 }
}

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Does anybody have experience of using mean-variance relationship in stan?  In the frequentist domain I found an article on this: http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378375810002764.  Is there some analog procedure in the Bayesian domain?  The problem I have in mind is related to counts and neither Poisson or negative binomial distribution provides satisfactory results.  For example, what to do if the Var[Y]=phi*E[Y]^lambda.  It would be great to estimate phi and lambda from the data.

Thank you,
Linas

messages.subject: open-ended survey modeling in stan
messages.subject_clean: open-ended survey modeling in stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I wonder if it is possible to design a survey where the survey open-ended questions are different for group A and group B?  The rationale is that we believe that group A will ignore some open-ended questions (subset A) while group B will ignore other open-ended questions (subset B).  To limit the survey size to make the survey questions more likely to be answered we give group A the survey without subset A and group B the survey without subset B.  Is it possible to analyze such non-balanced survey?

Thank you,
Linas

messages.subject: Very large fit objects in RStan
messages.subject_clean: Very large fit objects in RStan
messages.body_plain:
I am mystified by the size of fit objects in RStan. I just ran a model that had 23,000 data points and included an "ll" vector in transformed parameters to save the log likelihoods for a WAIC calculation. With 4 chains and 1000 sampling iterations and 8 bytes per value, that comes to 697 MB. The fit object, saved to disk, is much larger than that -- it is 3.9 GB. When I extract the samples from the fit object, I can verify (with object.size) that the sample size is what I expect. Even if the fit object is storing all the warmup samples too, that still leaves 2.5 GB unaccounted for. I'm having a hard time seeing how everything else a fit object might contain would add up to even a fraction of the size of the sample. (BTW, the data itself is less than 1 MB).

Can anyone offer some insight on this?

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] open-ended survey modeling in stan
messages.body_plain:
You can give people whatever questions you want --- it's an issue
of what you want to infer from their (non)answers.

It's only safe to do what you're suggesting if the answers from
groups A and B would be the same, which is presumably not the case
if they have different non-responses.

What you need to do is impute the missing data.  There
are whole books written on this topic, and others on the list know
this material much better than me.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
You can just use

  increment_log_prob(log_lik)

it's vectorized.

To make the model hierarchical, you replace your fixed priors on
A and B_raw with models for which you estimate the hierarchical
variance.

If at all possible, never apply exp() directly.  I see there's
an exp() on phi.  You could just use a lognormal, since you're
coding up a log normal indirectly, but that's probably not going
to help since there's an implicit exp() transform anyway.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Very large fit objects in RStan
messages.body_plain:
I'd guess it's related to the .MISC slot of the stanfit object.  My understanding is that it's an environment meant to hold the results of calculations of summary statistics, etc., so that they only need to be calculated once.  The environment is created in the sampling method of stanmodel:

> sfmiscenv <- new.env()

However, the default arguments of new.env (that is, parent = parent.frame() ) make the enclosing environment the environment associated with the evaluation of the sampling method, so when you save the fit object, you're also storing everything in that frame, which probably amounts to at least an additional copy of the samples and the data.

What's helped me in the past is to do something like the following manipulation of .MISC

> stanfit <- stan("model.stan", ...)
> stanfit@.MISC <- emptyenv()
> save(stanfit, file = "savefile.RData")
> ## New session
> load("savefile.Rdata")
> stanfit@.MISC <- new.env(parent = globalenv())

Now .MISC doesn't have the same enclosing environment as it originally had, and if I try to get the summary again it will need to be recalculated, but I didn't notice any problems with that.

A potential change to make the above workaround unnecessary would be to modify the source line above with sfmiscenv to specify a different enclosing environment ( globalenv() or emptyenv() )

Related from the serialization section of R internals manual:

> Serialization in R needs to take into account that objects may contain references to environments, which then have enclosing environments and so on. (Environments recognized as package or name space environments are saved by name.) There are ‘reference objects’ which are not duplicated on copy and should remain shared on unserialization. These are weak references, external pointers and environments other than those associated with packages, namespaces and the global environment. These are handled via a hash table, and references after the first are written out as a reference marker indexed by the table entry.

> Environments are treated in several ways: as we have seen, some are written as specific pseudo-SEXPTYPEs. Package and namespace environments are written with pseudo-SEXPTYPEs followed by the name. ‘Normal’ environments are written out as ENVSXPs with an integer indicating if the environment is locked followed by the enclosure, frame, ‘tag’ (the hash table) and attributes.

See also: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/13912867/empty-r-environment-becomes-large-file-when-saved

Even if the fit object is storing all the warmup samples too, that still leaves 2.5 GB unaccounted for. > On Apr 2, 2015, at 8:35 PM, Giorgio Paulon <giorgio...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Bob, that was a great help! Now my code is running much faster.
>
> I do have a couple of questions, though:
>
> (1)  I found the overflow issue: the critical line is
>
>       lambda[T_act] <- exp(eta' + X[T_act] * tau);
>
>       The calculation is much faster witout the exponentiation. However, a lot of warnings are raised because lambda is the parameter of a Poisson and, if a do not transformate lambda on a positive support, it can take negative values.
>       X is a matrix with non negative integers. However, I do not want to constrain the parameters eta and tau to a positive support, as they could take negative values. How can I avoid the problem of negative values of lambda (constraining the transformed
>       parameter lambda on a positive support does not work)?

You need to do something to keep those parameters positive.
But rather than writing

  lamba <- exp(gamma);
  y ~ poisson(lambda);

use

  y ~ poisson_log(lambda);

The _log takes the parameter on the log scale.

Or if you use functions, it's poisson_log_log() for the parameter on
the log scale version.  Sorry the notation's so confusing.  Adding
the _log was a bad decision I made very early on and haven't wanted
to change for fear of messing up everyone's existing models.

You want to make sure the support of the log probability function
defined by the model matches the constraints declared on any
parameters.

> (2)  Can the poisson_log and the bernoulli_logit_log functions be vectorized as their corresponding sampling statements?

The sampling statement

  y ~ foo(theta);

is roughly shorthand for

  increment_log_prob(foo_log(y,theta));

The difference is that the former drops constants.

So the foo_log() form will return a single value, which is
the sum of the probability function outputs if there are vector
inputs.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
So, I was running Stan from R and typing the usual thing:

stan(…, data=list(y=y, N=N, …))

or

stan(…, data=c(“y”,”N”,…))

And I realized (again) that R (or, I assume, Py and J and …) should be able to do this automatically by just reading off the variable names in the data block of the Stan program and looking for the objects in the workspace.  (And, if some of the objs are not there, they could be added in the call.)  Thus, e.g.,

stan(…) with no “data” argument would just pull everything out of the workspace and return an error if anything’s missing or is the wrong type

stan(…, data=list(y=y, N=50)) would use the specified data for y and N and pull all the other data out of the workspace, etc.

This would make a huge difference and should be really easy, no?

A

With lognormal you need to constrain the parameter to be positive.
And if you're initializing by hand, you need positive initial

> On Apr 4, 2015, at 7:55 AM, Linas Mockus <linasm...@gmail.com> wrote:

>

> - Did I make model hierarchical enough to handle very significant heteroscedasticity?

That's a different issue.  You need either a time series or
predictors of the variation.

> - How to compare poisson pseudo likelihood results with the ones from this model?  I want to prove to my frequuentist colleagues that Bayes is the way to go

I don't know what pseudolikelihood is.

We like to compare models using predictions, such as cross-validation.
But if they're frequentist they're probably not doing predictions
with their model estimates.

One of the main advantages of Bayesian inference is how simple it
is to do inference incorporating information about the data generating
process (scientific/domain-specific and measurement related).

> - How to check if heteroscedasticity is handled better than poisson pseudo likelihood

This would be rolled into any predictive evaluation.

> - Does it make sense to leave miu_phi parameter since it looks insignificant

It shouldn't hurt if you do full Bayesian inference and may
help with uncertainty.

> - Any other comments how to improve the code

Looks like it's mixing well as is.  I don't think those are the
traces that go with the model you sent, though, because there's no
little "a" in the model.  Also, you might want a fatter prior on
mu_A given that it's estimated value is around 10, though that's
still consistent with a normal(0,5) prior.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
> On Apr 4, 2015, at 5:36 PM, martina...@gmail.com wrote:

> Many thanks for the prompt reply. That's an elegant solution, in fact. I wonder however to which extent it will be able to deal with the risk of underestimation of the effect of the variables of interest upon the Pr(Y=1).

Underestimation is a form of bias where the expected value
of a parameter is less than the true value.  I think what
you're worried about is Pr[Y_n = 1 | data] being too low for cases
where Y_n = 1, which isn't quite the same thing.

In machine learning terms, Bayesian posteriors are based on
log loss, which is much less sensitive to category imbalance than
something like naive Bayes.  Even so, the overall objective function
is the log probabilty of the true categories given the model, so it
can still be an issue.

One thing you can do is artificially inflate the counts of one category
by repeating instances.  The effect is to overweight the overcounted
instances in the fit.  This will, in general have the opposite effect.

> I will play around with some prior specifications to see what happens. In any case, let me just ask a quick theoretical follow-up. If my predictors have not been scaled to be of order 1, then the best parameters for the informative prior in this case would be my expected value for the coefficient with a small sigma (but not too small so to approach the uninformative-ness)?

You want the prior to match what you expect the posterior to be.
If it's too small, it'll be overly informative, not uninformative,
but maybe you're thinking in terms of the BUGS/JAGS precision parameters.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Those aren't the same models.  In the JAGS model you use
a uniform(0,100) prior on the standard deviations whereas
in the Stan model you're using gamma(0.001,0.001).

I'm assuming you really mean to put this gamma prior on
precision (inverse square std dev), not on the std dev
parameter, because that would follow BUGS practice.

In our manual chapter on regression, you can find our own
recommended priors for these parameters.  You probably
want tighter priors on the b parameters and something
like cauchy(0, 2.5) on the sd parameters.  You have the
parameters properly constrained, so that shouldn't be a problem.
And you're using the bernoulli_logit, which is great.

To speed up Stan, there are two more things you can do.
One is to vectorize the priors, rewriting

 for (g in 1:G) {
    alpha[g] ~ normal(alpha_hat[g],sigma_alpha);
    b1[g] ~ normal(b1_hat[g],sigma_b1);
    b2[g] ~ normal(b2_hat[g],sigma_b2);
    alpha_hat[g] ~ normal(0, 100);
    b1_hat[g] ~ normal(0, 100);
    b2_hat[g] ~ normal(0, 100);
  }

as

  alpha ~ normal(mu_alpha, sigma_alpha);
  b1 ~ normal(b1_hat, sigma_b1);
  b2 ~ normal(b2_hat, sigma_b2);
  alpha_hat ~ normal(0, 100);
  b1_hat ~ normal(0, 100);
  b2_hat ~ normal(0, 100);

I'd also recommend changing the anmes --- "_hat" is typical
notation used for point estimates, not hierarchical priors.
We prefer something like:

  b1 ~ normal(mu_b1, sigma_b1);

so you're already halfway there!

Otherwise everything looks OK.  Are you trying to hand-initialize
the parameters?  If so, that may be another issue.  I'd try to let
Stan just do it automatically.

If you still have problems, please send us the data (or simulated
data) and the revised model.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
RStan should be coming to CRAN at some point in the hopefully not
too distant future.  Like everyone else, we have to first
satisfy the gatekeepers.  One piece of that puzzle is elimating
all vestiges of C++11, some of which are supported by all compilers
due to their being part of C, but are not officially part of C++03.

Here's the current numbering situation for the C++ version
of Stan:

2.6.1 was abandoned before a public release.

2.6.2 is the current official release behind the latest
RStan and PyStan.

2.6.3 has some very minor updates required to remove the last
vestiges of anti-CRAN behavior in Stan.  It's such a trivial update
it's not even worth mentioning other than that we hope it removed
the last traces of C++11.

See here:  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/releases

The scheme is Major.Minor.Patch.  Major versions introduce
major new features and/or break backward compatibility.  Minor
versions introduce minor features and bug patches and maintain
backward compatibility.  Patch releases just fix bugs without
adding new functionality.

RStan and PyStan and CmdStan follow Stan C++'s numbering.

RStan is still officially at 2.6.0.

PyStan has been updated to 2.6.3.

CmdStan has been updated to 2.6.2.

- Bob

Hi, I'm continuing this post <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/xv-Yjpb7faw/o7SHlrAH7sUJ> here as Bob recommended. I want to model RTs, and I suspect that a shifted lognormal hierarchical model is more accurate than just a lognormal hierarchical one. I've managed to fit the shifted lognormal model thanks to Bob, and I was hoping to get some advise regarding the model comparison.

As I said in the original post I thought about using WAIC (using this code <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/G9VuPvQchFY/CXPK9fV9BHoJ>).

    log_lik[i] <- normal_log(rt[i]-c[i],log_mu[i], sigma);

There's something wrong for sure, because I get a huge WAIC for the shifted lognormal, even though I simulated the data with a lognormal distribution (in fakedata.Rda). If I understood Bob correctly, it may have to do with having an extra parameter that varies by subject (the shift) in the shifted model, which I don't have in the other lognormal model. I think I may have read somewhere that one shouldn't compare different distributions with WAIC, but in any case, I'm not sure if it's right, and if I really have different distributions (in the lognormal one, the shift is 0).

Any recommendation on how to compare the models would be much appreciated!
Bruno

messages.body_plain:
If you're doing likelihood evaluations, you typically want to marginalize
out any latent parameters associated with data items.

The most general way of doing evaluations is cross-validation.  Estimate
the model on part of the data and predict the rest.  You want to use full
Bayes for that --- the generated quantities block in Stan is set up to do that.
It can also be tricky with hierarchical data or time series, because you
can't just take a random subset of the data.

- Bob

Did you try simulating data according to the model then trying
to fit that?  We recommend always doing that before trying to
fit real data.

We'd also generally recommend starting with a small model that
does fit and gradually increasing its complexity.  Then you can
diagnose where things go wrong.  It's hard to debug a large
model that doesn't work.

When you say the model gets stuck in the first iteration, what is
happening?   And you haven't set refresh=1, so you can't be sure it's
really the first iteration that's the problem.

One thing you can do to try to debug is add print() statements to
track the values of variables.

How much memory do you have on your machine?  Is it possible that it
tries to swap to disk and isn't technically stuck, but just going very
slowly?

Are you letting Stan do the initialization?  If not, I'd try that
first.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Maja & welcome to the Stan list.

I can't help you with the PyStan, but you're the
second person to ask about this Auction model --- sounds
like it's part of the PPAML task.

But I can comment on the model itself --- see below.

> On Apr 6, 2015, at 11:58 AM, Maja Rudolph <marir...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I am using PyStan to fit a model to auction data. I get a value error for variable __header__ in pystan/misc.py
> Any hints what can be causing this error?
> Below are the error message as well as the model code.
>
> INFO:pystan:COMPILING THE C++ CODE FOR MODEL anon_model_07b8cf1021ff43e6843005b4d44744e6 NOW.
> Traceback (most recent call last):
>   File "ovr_stan.py", line 76, in <module>
>     iter=1000, chains=4)
>   File "/usr/local/lib/python2.7/dist-packages/pystan/api.py", line 385, in stan
>     n_jobs=n_jobs, **kwargs)
>   File "/usr/local/lib/python2.7/dist-packages/pystan/model.py", line 685, in sampling
>     fit = self.fit_class(data)
>   File "stanfit4anon_model_07b8cf1021ff43e6843005b4d44744e6_996311c807219e4458bfdda0257145f8.pyx", line 426, in stanfit4anon_model_07b8cf1021ff43e6843005b4d44744e6_996311c807219e4458bfdda0257145f8.StanFit4Model.__cinit__ (/tmp/tmpsuFrsU/pystan/stanfit4anon_model_07b8cf1021ff43e6843005b4d44744e6_996311c807219e4458bfdda0257145f8.cpp:7834)
>   File "/usr/local/lib/python2.7/dist-packages/pystan/misc.py", line 366, in _split_data
>     raise ValueError(msg.format(k))
> ValueError: Variable __header__ is neither int nor float nor list/array thereof
>
>
> ovr_code = """
> functions{
>     real revenue(real y, real B, real b) {
>         real rev;
>         rev <- if_else(y>b, y, b);
>         rev <- if_else(B>y, 0, rev);
>         return rev;
>     }
> }

I'd code this as follows, but your tastes may vary:

  if (B > y) return 0;
  if (y > b) return y;
  return b;

> data {
>     int<lower=0> N;                            // number of observations
>     int<lower=1> d;                            // number of dimensions
>     matrix[N,d] x;                               // covariates
>     vector[N] B;                                 // highest bid
>     vector[N] b;                                  // second bid
>     int<lower=0,upper=1> z[N];            // hallucinated data
> }
> parameters {
>     real w0;                // intercept
>     vector[d] w;            // weight vector
>     real<lower=0> sigma;    // std
>     vector[N] y;            // reserve price
>
> }
> model {
>     y ~ normal(w0 + x*w, sigma);
>     for (i in 1:N)
>      z[i] ~ bernoulli(exp(-revenue(y[i],B[i],b[i])));
> }

I take it the inferential goal here is to estimate the reserve price
y and covariates w and w0.

Stan's going to potentially have problems with this model because
of the discontinuity in y due to the revenue() function not being
smooth.

Also, if you wanted to do a logistic regression rather than using
the non-stand link function, it'd be:

  for (i in 1:N)

    z[i] ~ bernoulli_logit(-revenue(y[i], B[i], b[i]));

You're also going to have to be careful that z[i] == 1 whenever
revenue(y[i], B[i], b[i]) = 0.  So make sure it's a focused
hallucination!

- Bob

Aki

messages.body_plain:
Have you tried to fit with data simulated from the model? If not, could
you do that to make sure both programs can recover the proper parameter
values?

It's hard to debug a big program that's not working, whereas it's much
easier to build up a simpler program that works and see where it fails.

The Stan and JAGS models are still different in terms of priors and
constraints, but I don't see any reason the Stan model should be so slow
relative to the JAGS models unless the model is extremely poorly specified
(statistically, not computationally).   In some cases where the posterior
is improper or nearly improper, Gibbs will merrily iterate without
actually sampling from the posterior.

Could you let Stan run fewer iterations and see what the diagnostic
parameters are, such as tree depth and acceptance?   A high treedepth
(near or pegged at 10) will indicate a problem in the posterior.
In which case, it's likely JAGS isn't behaving properly either, just
running quick iterations.  Did the draws from JAGS look like they converged
in terms of R-hat and n_eff?

Given that the variable names are different, are you sure you're
running the same data and sizes of data?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I just simulated the data and found your problem.
Your hierarchical prior parameters are vectors rather than
scalars.  This will cause the model to not be identified
and Stan will march all over the "posterior", whereas Gibbs
will move in a random walk, making it seem like Gibbs is
sampling from the posterior.

There's a more thorough discussion in the problematic posteriors
section of the manual with a very simple example involving normal
location (mean) parameters.

When I fix that problem and simulate data with N = 1000 and G=10,
Stan recovers the simulated parameters within their 95% intervals
in roughly 40 seconds using default settings.

I'm attaching both my simulator and the revised model.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I apologize if this posts out of order - it makes me reply to the first post not the recent additions.

Did getting rid of the loop in the parameters block make the code run? If not, note that the indexing variable in the loop was lower case - get rid of the loop and make the array of ordered logistic vectors size K and try again.

I am using the ordered_logistic statement for a GRM model as well and have no problems. Here is my code:

model.stereo <- "
  data{
    int<lower=2, upper=4> K; // four number of categoies
    int N; // 1803 number of individuals
    int D; // 7 number of items
    int<lower=1,upper=K> Y[N,D]; //array of responses
  }
  parameters {
    real<lower=0> slope[D]; // slope
    ordered[K-1] c[D]; //intercepts
    vector[N] theta; // latent trait
  }
  model{
    slope ~ cauchy(0,5);
    theta ~ normal(0,1);

    for (n in 1:N)

      for (d in 1:D)
        Y[n,d] ~ ordered_logistic(theta[n]*slope[d],c[d]);
  }
"

The differences from your code and mine is that I have no missing data (so I don't need to use the database-style coding), I use a cauchy prior on the slope instead of a normal prior with a hyperparameter variance (I'm confused why you use that type of a prior but to each his own), and I do not place a prior on the ordered intercepts (the data find them perfectly fine without them).

One important note, though, is that the ordered_logistic distribution uses eta minus intercept, whereas other IRT programs (mirt-package, IRTPro, FlexMIRT) use eta plus intercept. To compare results with other programs you need to know this and flip the sign on all intercepts (order and values stay the same).

Hope that helps!
Aaron

messages.body_plain:
My apologies -- you are correct. More information would be useful. Below I've included comments throughout the code. I ended up testing it on the Science data in the R ltm package. It consists of four five category items. I realize that Stan cannot yet accommodate ragged arrays, but the number of categories is constant by item here (and in my work), so the vector of response categories by item could just as easily be changed to a scalar where K=4. Other than that, I think the comments will help. If not, please let me know. And thanks in advance for the help. It's much appreciated.
require(ltm)
require(rjags)

data<-Science[c(1,3,4,7)]
data<-cbind(as.numeric(data[,1]),as.numeric(data[,2]), as.numeric(data[,3]), as.numeric(data[,4]) )

N<-length(data[,1]) #N rows
P<-length(data[1,]) #N items
K<-apply(data,2,max, na.rm=T) # This could be stored as a scalar, since K is the same for each item.
data.1 <- list(y=data,N=N,p=P,K=K)

modelstring <- "
model{
  for(i in 1:N){ #Loop over respondent,
    for (j in 1:p){ #Loop over item

      y[i,j]~dcat(prob[i,j,1:K[j]])
    }

    theta[i]~dnorm(0, 1) #Latent ability
    for (j in 1:p){ #Loop over item
      for (k in 1:(K[j]-1)){ #Loop through K-1 response categories
        logit(P[i,j,k])<-kappa[j,k]-alpha[j]*theta[i]
      }
      P[i,j,K[j]]<-1
    }
    for (j in 1:p){ #Loop over item
      prob[i,j,1]<-P[i,j,1]
      for (k in 2:K[j]){ #Loop through K-1 response categories

        prob[i,j,k]<-P[i,j,k]-P[i,j,k-1]
      }
    }
  }
  #Specify priors/hyperpriors for alpha

  for (j in 1:p){

    alpha[j]~dnorm(mu,prec)
  }

  mu~dnorm(1,0.01)I(0,) #This censors the alpha parameters
  prec~dgamma(1,.1)

  for (j in 1:p){

    kappa0[j,1]~dunif(-10,10)

    for (k in 2:K[j]-1){

      kappa0[j,k]~dunif(kappa0[j,k-1],10)

    }
    kappa[j,1:K[j]-1]<-sort(kappa0[j,1:K[j]-1])
  }
}
"

model<-tempfile()
cat(modelstring,file=model)
rats.inits.2 <- function(){
  list("alpha"=rep(1, times=4),
       "kappa0"=matrix(rep(c(1:3), each=4), nrow=4)
  )
}
m <- jags.model(file=model,  data=data.1, n.chains=3, n.adapt=1000, inits=rats.inits.2)
draws <- coda.samples(m, 1000, variable.names=c("alpha", "kappa", "theta"), 10)

> I just simulated the data and found your problem.
> Your hierarchical prior parameters are vectors rather than
> scalars.  This will cause the model to not be identified
> and Stan will march all over the "posterior", whereas Gibbs
> will move in a random walk, making it seem like Gibbs is
> sampling from the posterior.
>
> There's a more thorough discussion in the problematic posteriors
> section of the manual with a very simple example involving normal
> location (mean) parameters.
>
> When I fix that problem and simulate data with N = 1000 and G=10,
> Stan recovers the simulated parameters within their 95% intervals
> in roughly 40 seconds using default settings.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical logistic regression on sparse data
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Hierarchical logistic regression on sparse data
messages.body_plain:
These models are tricky to estimate without informative priors
when data is sparse.  The true posterior winds up being close to
the prior, so if you use a very diffuse "BUGS-like" prior such as
inv_gamma(0.001,0.001), or uniform(0,1000) or something like that,
you'll run into statistical problems as well as computational
ones.  It's what Andrew calls "the Folk Theorem":

  http://andrewgelman.com/2009/05/24/handy_statistic/

Why are you specifying Sigma as data rather than estimating it?
There are recommendations for priors and how to estimate it in
our manual chapter on regression.  If you really want a fixed
diagonal covariance prior, then just use independent priors --- the
multivariate versions are computationally costly.

- Bob

P.S.  Andrew --- Lisa's already using sd appropriately --- variance
is sampled inverse gamma and then the sqrt of variance used in the normal.

messages.subject: How to use the posterior sample obtained for parameters as prior for another model?
messages.subject_clean: How to use the posterior sample obtained for parameters as prior for another model?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Everybody,
1. Let us say I have 3 models A,B,C and I want to use posterior obtained from Model A as prior to parameters in models B and C (B and C are different stan files). One easy way is to just obtain the mean and variance of the posterior of model A and use a gaussian prior with those parameters. Is there a better way to do this?

2. Let us say I have model posterior of whose parameters are simulated via a sampling by providing data D1 after some time I obtain new data D2 can I update HMC sampling chain with new observed data D2 or should I rerun the HMC to convergence with data D1+D2 in one shot?

3. What I would also like to know is, does the sampling-chain store all the data that was used to converge it internally ? or does it summarize it in some way? My intuition says it actually stores all the data that was used to run the chain to convergence and I am just hoping my intuition is wrong as this would seriously limit how I can update the model in an online fashion. I would love to hear advice on how one would go about solving such a problem.

Thanks,
Sunil.

> On Apr 7, 2015, at 2:43 PM, Sunil S Nandihalli <sunil.na...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Everybody,
> 1. Let us say I have 3 models A,B,C and I want to use posterior obtained from Model A as prior to parameters in models B and C (B and C are different stan files). One easy way is to just obtain the mean and variance of the posterior of model A and use a gaussian prior with those parameters. Is there a better way to do this?

Fit everything jointly.  Everything else is an approximation.
(Though technically with M posterior draws for A, you could use
those to run M fits for B, and so on, but you'll run into
serious combinatorial problems that way.)

> 2. Let us say I have model posterior of whose parameters are simulated via a sampling by providing data D1 after some time I obtain new data D2 can I update HMC sampling chain with new observed data D2

There is no way to do that soundly.

> or should I rerun the HMC to convergence with data D1+D2 in one shot?

You should rerun everything.

> 3. What I would also like to know is, does the sampling-chain store all the data that was used to converge it internally ? or does it summarize it in some way? My intuition says it actually stores all the data that was used to run the chain to convergence and I am just hoping my intuition is wrong as this would seriously limit how I can update the model in an online fashion. I would love to hear advice on how one would go about solving such a problem.

Which interface are you talking about and what do you mean by "sampling-chain"?

Stan runs MCMC in two phases:

  1. a warmup phase that estimates step size and mass matrix, and

  2. a sampling phase that draws from the posterior using estimated
     step size and mass matrix from warmup phase.

The warmup draws do not constitute a Markov chain and shouldn't
be used for inference.

The output of all of the interfaces store the results of adaptation, but
we don't currently have a way to read those back in for a warm start.  (It's
on our to-do list and we should get to it this year, we hope.)

- Bob

> On Apr 7, 2015, at 3:13 PM, Lisa Mu <lisa...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi,Bob:
>
> #1. I will take your advice to use independent N(0,sd=100) for beta. Since random effects are focus, I use a simple distribution on beta.

My advice was just that it's quite a bit faster in terms of
computation to use this

  theta ~ normal(0, sigma);

for theta of size N rather than the equivalent

  theta ~ multi_normal(rep_vector(0, N),
                       sigma * diag_matrix(rep_vector(0,N)));

We recommend a value of sigma that matches the problem, not
one of the BUGS-style super-diffuse priors.  This is what
Andrew calls "weakly informative", though there's not a precise
definition.  For instance, if you expect your values of
theta to be roughly in (-1,1), then a normal(0,5) is "weakly
informative."  If you go to normal(0,100), you might as well
just use an improper uniform prior.   You can substitute a Cauchy
for the normal if you want to allow the occasional outlier.

> #2 If the model is sensitive to prior, then as "the Folk Theorem" you pointed out, there is something wrong with the model. In real case, the sparse data could reflect limited spatial clusters between A and B. I am not sure how to incorporate this information into the model.

All models are sensitive to the prior in some form or another
because it affects the form of the posterior.  It's just a quantitative
matter of how much.  Of course, with a fixed prior, more data will wash
out the prior.

If you actually have information about the problem (and almost
everyone does before they start), then you want to include it in
the prior or the likelihood.

Also, the folk theorem is heavily hedged in saying there *may* be
something wrong with your model.  There are legitimate models that
are hard to compute.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
abs(a) is continuous, just not continously differentiable.
Same for sqrt(a^2).

You can get close with a "soft" absolute value that is
equal to abs(a) except for a small neighborhood around 0
where it's smoothed out.

But that doesn't help with the other issue that abs(a) creates,
namely that it introduces a reflection-based multimodality
if a is a parameter.

What's the purpose of that log_diff_exp_abs function you're
proposing?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Yes, I just calculated the diff myself and came to the same conclusion. I will look at the coth stuff, thanks.

The purpose of the log_diff_exp_abs function is to be able to calculate what is called the "Bateman" function, i.e. in PK systems you often have the following form:

1/(a-b) * ( exp(-a*t) - exp(-b*t))

If a > b, then everything is straightforward. If a < b the result is still always positive, but using log_diff_exp does not work, as a - b is negative and hence only the total expression remains positive.

Doing this squaring and root thing solves the issue.

Sebastian

PS: I just had to find out, that the Bateman function seems to be, in general, differently defined if you refer to mathworld: http://mathworld.wolfram.com/BatemanFunction.html

messages.subject: Logistic GP
messages.subject_clean: Logistic GP
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm testing out a fairly straightforward model. The basic idea is to assess how likely it is someone will purchase on a particular day, given time since last purchase (interpurchase time). Traditionally, hazard models are used for this sort of thing, but I'm testing instead using Gaussian Processes to estimate a latent "propensity to buy" function, where purchases are binary variables modeled as a bernoulli_logit of the propensity. Basically, the data are a string of 1's or 0's, with 1 indicating purchase, and with an associated interpurchase time counter, so a typical section of the data might look like:

P:  0 0 1   |   0 0 0 0 1   |    0 ...
T:  1 2 3   |   1 2 3 4 5   |   1 ...

In my simulations, there are 500 customers, tracked for 50 days. The GP has interpurchase time as its only input, so we're estimating a latent function f(t), where t=1,...,50 (and thus the covariance matrix is 50x50).

In the code attached, I use a parametric form to set this latent function, then try to recover it with a GP specification like done in the stan manual. The first concern is that the model takes forever to run, but this isn't ultimately why I'm posting. The major concern is that, depending on whether or not I estimate the parameters of the covariance function, I get wildly different results.

More specifically, I start by doing a full analysis on everything, estimating both the latent function and the hyperparameters of the covariance function (called "gpp_simple" in the code). Once that estimation finishes running, I take the median of the estimated hyperparameters, then fix the covariance function with those values. I then estimate the GP again (called "gpp_spec2"). The results make little sense:
In the full estimation case, I get results that make sense, especially when interpreted on the "probability" scale instead of the latent function scale. The two plots are numbered 1 and 2, attached, where the mean of the estimation is in black, and the truth is in red dotted.
In the fixed hyperparameters case, I get nonsense results for about half of the time periods--it starts out looking fine, then goes crazy. These results are numbered 3 and 4, attached, where again the mean of the estimation is in black, and the truth is in red dotted.
So basically, the latent function is recovered in the more uncertain case, where I let stan estimate the hyperparameters, but is not recovered when I fix the hyperparameters at reasonable values (I should add that I've tried a wide range of values--this happens consistently). I'm not an expert in GPs by any means, so it's possible there's something I'm missing theoretically.

One thing to note: as you can tell in the attached graphics, the model works for the first several time periods. It also seems to work if I limit the number of time periods to just that number---say, t.max=20. More than that, though, and it goes crazy. At 50, the problem is most clearly evident. Things get even crazier, though, as t.max gets higher. Typically, I would attribute that to a problem with many inputs, since the time period is the only input to the GP, but it doesn't explain why the model works, regardless of t.max (and slow run time), if I allow estimation of the hyperparameters, instead of fixing them at their (previously estimated) values.

Any help would be much appreciated! Specifically looking to understand why this might be happening--an error in my understand of GPs/stan, or a stan error/quirk of some kind.

Thanks,
Ryan

Cool.  We (Andrew and I) were speculating (without the
theoretical knowhow to back it up) that the data would
overwhelm the tails of the simple transform.

I still think there's a lot to be written about which
transforms to use.  This kind of stuff's priceless, but
it seems maybe a bit too complicated to put in the manual.
On the other hand, without it, and without understanding it,
I don't know how people are supposed to understand what's
going on with the tools they're using.

I need a year to study manifolds!

- Bob

> On Apr 9, 2015, at 12:14 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Lemme explain what’s going on theoretically.
>
> When we transform to an unconstrained scale the posterior density picks
> up a Jacobian which manifests as a new contribution to the potential
> energy in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo.  When we use a logit transformation
> this contribution is
>
> V = log(1 + cosh(x)) + const,
>
> which is essentially just a smoothed version of the Laplace distribution.
> If we use the inverse-Phi transformation, on the other hand, we get
> a quadratic potential,
>
> V = 0.5 * x^{2} + const.
>
> Now _both_ of these potential energies yield well-behaved trajectories
> for HMC (HMC with either a static or dynamic integration time is
> geometrically ergodic for both!).  The problem with the logit-induced
> potential energy is that the period of the trajectory increases out in
> the tails while the period of the inverse-Phi-induced trajectories is
> constant.  What this means is that out in the tails the logit-induced
> trajectories need to evolve for a much longer time to cover the same
> distance, which is why the number of leapfrog steps increased
> relative to the inverse-Phi trajectories.
>
> This is the general problem with heavy-tailed target distributions,
> by the way.  As you get out in the tails the gradients get smaller
> which causes the momenta to decrease and you need to integrate
> for longer and longer to explore each level set.  Eventually the
> gradients get so weak that you’re not even guaranteed to come
> back to the bulk (exactly when this happens is an open research
> question).
>
> Anyways, in a 1D problem where you have only the Jacobians
> the inverse-Phi transformation is indeed expected to have better
> performance.  Of course that’s not the typical situation in which
> we’re in!  The original density will change the tails and wash
> much of this behavior out, and in more than one dimension
> chaos arises and things get even more complicated.  Then
> there’s the computational issues of needing the inverse-Phi
> function to handle initializations and the like.
>
> But if you have parameters with upper and lower bounds
> and suspect that you might have consequent heavy tails
> (you can also check this by plotting lp vs the number of leapfrog
> steps — if the number of leapfrog steps increases as lp decreases
> then you know that you have heavy tails) then it might be worth
> trying the inverse-Phi transform instead of the default logit-transform.
>
>

Yes, in theory jitter is not needed. In practice it may help a lot without changing the model. Radford Neal* writes that a small amount of jitter (e.g. 0.01)  alters the logistic model only slightly. A larger amount of jitter (e.g. 10) will make the model to perform as probit model, and you could even make the amount of jitter to be a hyperparameter.

* Radford Neal. Regression and classification using Gaussian process priors. In Bayesian Statistics 6, Bernardo et al (eds), pp. 475-501, Oxford University Press, 1998.

I'm interested to know how fast your inference is now with the larger amount of jitter?

Aki

Thanks Herra Huu!

When thinking possible prior choices for the jitter, the problem is that we are willing to move away from logit model to get faster sampling, and then the choice of prior is not based on our prior knowledge (or lack-of knowledge).

If ignoring the computational speed, it might be helpful to think that probit corresponds to latent Gaussian and logit is close to latent Student-t with nu=7. The model with the jitter hyperparameter will have these as limits.

Aki

messages.body_plain:
At the moment, this doesn't seem particularly feasible. The function formerly known as testify() throws away everything but the user-defined functions and makes a lot of changes to those anyway. But if you do

cat(stanc("model.stan", obfuscate_name = FALSE), file = "model.cpp", sep = "\n")

then you have a C++ file in your working directory that could be part of a package. You would just have to do a bit of work to export the relevant C++ functions and write R functions that called the C++ functions. To some extent this would be scriptable but there are no scripts yet.

Ben

On Sunday, June 23, 2013 at 12:23:28 PM UTC-7, Jackson King wrote:
>
> Hello,
>
>
> I am estimating a simple graded response model (4 items, each with four categories). I have slightly modified a model that runs in JAGS to run in STAN, but am encountering some problems. I am wondering if anybody can provide some pointers.
>
>
> Below is everything, including the data from the ltm package.
>
>
> I would be greatly appreciative for some help.
>
>
> Thanks
>
>
>
> require(ltm)
>
> data<-Science[c(1,3,4,7)]
>
> data<-cbind(as.numeric(data[,1]),as.numeric(data[,2]), as.numeric(data[,3]), as.numeric(data[,4]) )
>
> n<-length(data[,1])
>
> p<-length(data[1,])
>
> K<-apply(data,2,max, na.rm=T)
>
>
> data.1 <- list(y=data,n=n,p=p,K=K)
>
>
> grm_code<-"
>
> data {
>
>        int<lower=0> n; //Number of participants
>
>        int<lower=0> p; //Number of items
>
>        int<lower=0> K; //Number of categories per item
>
>        int<lower=1,upper=4> y[n]; //Data
>
> }
>
> parameters {
>
>   real theta[n]; // ability for n
>
>   ordered[K-1] tau[p]; // difficulty for the item
>
>   real<lower=0> alpha[p];// discrimination parameter for the item
>
>   real<lower=0> sigma_tau; // sd of abilities
>
>   real<lower=0> sigma_alpha; // sd of difficulties
>
>   }
>
> model{
>
> real Q[n, p, 3];
>
> real prob[n, p, 4];
>
> theta~normal(0, 1);
>
> tau ~ cauchy(0,sigma_tau);
>
> alpha~cauchy(0, sigma_alpha);
>
> sigma_tau~cauchy(0,5);
>
> sigma_alpha~cauchy(0,5);
>
>  for(i in 1:n){
>
>     for (j in 1:p){
>
>         for (k in 1:(K[j]-1)){
>
>          Q[i,j,k]<-inv_logit(alpha[j]*(theta[i]-tau[j,k]));
>
>       }
>
>   prob[i,j,1]<-1-Q[i,j,1];
>
>          for (k in 2:(K[j]-1))
>
>   prob[i,j,k]<-prob[i,j,k-1]-prob[i,j,k];
>
>   prob[i,j,K[j]]<-Q[i,j,K[j]-1];
>
>   y[i,j]~categorical(prob[i,j,1:K[j]]);
>
> }
>
>   }
>
>  }
>
> "
>
>
> fit <- stan(model_code = grm_code,
>
>             data = data.1, iter = 1000, chains = 2)
>
>
>
>

This seems to work. When I remove the loop from the parameters, the model produces estimates quite similar to grm in the ltm package. Thanks. I really appreciate all the help with this.

On Sunday, Ju

I agree with Sebastian.  I’m simulating a lot of fake data and I’d love to be able to routinely to do this in Stan rather than having to write custom R code. Sebastian told me that there’s a function, I think Ben wrote, that allows you to run Stan functions from R.   Using functions should be more convenient than having to write an entire Stan program with an empty model block.  It is not urgent, I just think it will be very helpful.

Using the generated quantities block is perfect for simulation _after_ inference, but it’s not the most natural thing for simulating fake data from the prior, or for simulating new quantities given simulations from a previously-fitted model.  For the latter, Daniel suggested a hack in R, but it should be possible to do it more directly.

messages.body_plain:
For the case in question, I had only interval bounds on some durations that fed into a Poisson model. That is, I had something similar to

    x[i] ~ poisson(lambda * t[i]);

where the precise value of t[i] is not known. I had a simple model of the durations

    t[i] ~ exponential(theta);

and a known upper and lower bound for each t[i]. So, yes, the t[i] are weakly constrained within the interval. They are not, however, what I'm really interested in -- it's lambda that interests me. (This is all a simplification of the actual model, which is actually a multilevel Poisson regression.)

> I modified these slightly to make theta and theta_raw be vectors of 10,000 elements. The first model (default transformation) took 225.508 seconds. The second model (normal cdf transformation) took half that time -- 122.82 seconds.
>
> On Tuesday, April 7, 2015 at 9:05:44 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Thanks!  I'm hoping Michael will weigh in on this one.
>
> I was just talking about doing some experiments with transforms
> and efficiency yesterday.
>
> I did verify your curvature calculation;  Wolfram Alpha
> even reproduced your plot as an added bonus:
>
> http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=d%2Fdx+%28d+%28log+%28exp%28-x%29+%2F+%281+%2B+exp%28-x%29%29%5E2%29%29+%2F+dx%29
>
> What I'd like to see is a basic empirical evaluation of these two
> models:
>
>   parameters {
>     real<lower=0,upper=1> theta;
>   }
>   model {
>   }
>
> and
>
>   parameters {
>     real theta_raw;
>   }
>   transformed parameters {
>     real<lower=0,upper=1> theta;
>     theta <- Phi(theta_raw);
>   }
>   model {
>     theta_raw ~ normal(0,1);
>   }
>
> because that will isolate the effect of just the transform we
> use.  It's basically the difference between sampling from the logistic
> distribution and the normal distribution.
>
> The normal is nice in that its log density has constant curvature
> for fixed sigma.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Apr 8, 2015, at 12:48 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
> >
> > Wow! That's great!
> >
> > On Tue, Apr 7, 2015 at 10:38 PM, Kevin Van Horn <ke...@ksvanhorn.com> wrote:
> > From time to time I need to deal with a model that involves a latent variable that is constrained to lie within an interval. For example, I am currently working with a model that has duration as an independent variable, but the duration is only known roughly -- I have upper and lower bounds on it.  I introduce a latent "duration" variable for each observation, constrained to lie within the bounds for that observation.
> >
> > The problem is that these models always run excruciatingly slowly in Stan. On this current example it was taking so long that I had to dial down to only 100 iterations total (50 burnin, 50 sampling) just to get some sort of output I could look at to diagnose the problem. Those 100 iterations took 4814 seconds (72 minutes). Taking a look at the sampler parameters, I saw that n_leapfrog__ had an average value of 1454. Ouch!
> >
> > Thinking about it for a bit, I realized what the problem is. If I understand correctly, HMC and NUTS work best when the curvature of the log probability density is nearly constant, as this means that the same step size is optimal in all parts of the posterior. But the transformation that Stan uses for interval-constrained variables -- inverse logit -- introduces a Jacobian adjustment term whose curvature varies wildly, from -1/2 when x=0 (where x is the unconstrained variable) and falling to 0 as |x| gets large (see attached image). If you have 23000 interval-constrained latent variables, this is a big problem.
> >
> > The solution is to use the normal CDF to transform from the unconstrained to the constrained variable. Its derivative is the normal density, the log of that is a quadratic function, and the curvature of a quadratic function is constant -- perfect for HMC!
> >
> > To be specific, I replaced
> >
> >     parameters {
> >       vector<lower=0, upper=1>[N] y0;
> >       ....
> >     }
> >     transformed parameters {
> >       vector[N] y;
> >       y <- lower_bound + (upper_bound - lower_bound) .* y0;
> >       ...
> >     }
> >
> > with
> >
> >     parameters {
> >       vector[N] x;
> >       ....
> >     }
> >     transformed parameters {
> >       vector[N] y;
> >       for (i in 1:N)
> >         y[i] <- lower_bound[i] + (upper_bound[i] - lower_bound[i]) * normal_cdf(x[i], 0, 1);
> >       ...
> >     }
> >     model {
> >       increment_log_prob(-0.5 * dot_self(x));
> >       ...
> >     }
> >
> > The result: the time for those 100 iterations went down by a factor of 2.9 (!) and the average value for n_leap__ went down by a factor of 2.2, to 655.
> >
> > This suggests that maybe the normal CDF instead of inverse logit should be the transform that Stan uses for interval-constrained variables.
> >
> >
> >

parameters...

	real CL[jend];
	real V1[jend];
	real V2[jend];

model ...

If you declare the parameters with <lower=0>, that error will
go away.

> But is it not implicit that a lognormal parameters is always >0?

No!  Stan is not BUGS or JAGS.  You need to declare the parameters
with constraints that matches their support in the model.

The error message you sent was because the lognormal didn't have
positive-constrained parameters.

You still have problems, such as a parameter

	real tauCL;

declared to range over (-inf,inf), but a sampling statement

	tauCL~gamma(CLa,CLb);

with support (0, inf).  They need to match.

- Bob

On Thursday, April 9, 2015 at 10:07:56 PM UTC+2, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> I agree with Sebastian.  I’m simulating a lot of fake data and I’d love to be able to routinely to do this in Stan rather than having to write custom R code.  One very pleasant thing about simulation in Stan is that it treats everything as a random variable, hence no need to loop over #sims, no more rnorm(nsims,…), etc.  This could be a very big deal!

Hi,

This is for this sort of stuff that I wrote gsim. I think the current interface is a bit

>
>> But is it not implicit that a lognormal parameters is always >0?
>
> No!  Stan is not BUGS or JAGS.  You need to declare the parameters
> with constraints that matches their support in the model.

Perhaps to clarify this last point of Bob’s:  in Stan, there is no such thing as “a lognormal parameter.”  If your model block has a statement:

x ~ lognormal(0,1);

This does _not_ mean that x is lognormally distributed.  It does not even mean that x has a lognormal prior.  _All_ that is meant by this line of code is that the log of the lognormal density is added to the log posterior at this step.  That’s all.

messages.body_plain:
What Ben says!   Using

  E[y^2] - E[y]^2

The point is never ever do subtractions when you don't have
to because you can lose arbitrary amounts of precision when the
numbers are close to each other.   For example, if the numbers
are close to each other, as in

1.1111 - 1.1110 = .0001

you go from five digits of precision down to 1.
You also have underflow issues, so that

1 - 1e-16 == 1

So you lose either the amount of shared prefix if they're close
or the difference if they're far away.  Subtraction is just bad news
for floating point numbers.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Maybe I'm misunderstanding who's saying what, so let me
start from first principles.

Calculating as

  E[y^2] - E[y]^2 = 1/N SUM_n y[n]^2  - (1/N SUM_n y[n])^2

only involves a single subtraction and that subtraction
has to be done, whereas

  E[(y - E[y])^2]  =  1/N SUM_n (y - E[y])^2

involves N subtractions.

For scalars, of course, you can just use var(y).  It's for vectors
that we don't have something built in and for that we should have a covar()
function built in with custom gradients that implements the result and
gradients stably so users don't have to worry about it.

- Bob

P.S.   I think arithmetic stability of Stan code is a reasonable user-facing
       issue, but feel free to move to stan-dev if you'd prefer.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Continuing sampling
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Continuing sampling
messages.body_plain:
I need to add some description of this to the manual, because
this keeps coming up.

You absolutely cannot just keep going.  Nor do you want to.
The problem is that if you haven't reached convergence, then
you want to do more warmup, and then more sampling.  So you'd
have to toss out the sampling part of the run anyway.

Andrew's the one who urged us to do it this way in the first
place based on the following argument.

If you run 1000 warmup iterations and 1000 sampling iterations
and haven't converged, then you want to go back and run
2000 warmup iterations and 2000 sampling iterations.  If you
were to restart, after the original warmup iterations, you'd save
around 15% of your work.  Here's an example with the default
number of iterations (which is probably way too high):

rerun from the beginning

   1000 + 1000
   2000 + 2000
   -----------
   3000 + 3000

rewarmup:

   1000     + 1000
   0 + 1000 + 2000
   -----------
   2000 + 3000

The exception to this is when you have converged during warmup, but
just haven't drawn enough iterations for the n_eff you need.  In that
case, you'd get this:

 resample:

   1000 + 1000
      0 + 1000
   -----------
   3000

 restart:

   1000 + 1000
   1000 + 2000
   -----------
   5000

So you'd save about 40% of your total effort if you could just run more
samples.

- Bob

P.S.  I don't know about "soon" --- there's a huge backlog on our
to-do list.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Speed up the code
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Speed up the code
messages.body_plain:
The problem at this point is likely that your ODE is stiff, which
is not something Stan can handle at this point.  You can try to
deal with this in one of two ways

1.  Use a smaller initial stepsize and a higher target accept rate, e.g.,
    for RStan, add an argument

    control=list(stepsize=0.01, adapt_delta=0.99)

2.  Use reasonable inits for parameters.  You can either put these in by
    hand if you have reasonable guesses, or if centered inits on the unconstrained
    scale are reasonable (after transforms based on constraints;  e.g., positive constrained is
    log transformed), then you can try to init at 0, with

    init=0

Otherwise, if it is a stiffness in the ODE, you'll have to wait until we
add a stiff ODE solver.  That's one of our highest priorities at the moment,
so it should be out reasonably soon (as in the next six months, not the next
few days).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I think the issue is that Andrew wants everything written in Stan,
ideally just once.  What we want to avoid is any code duplication
at all.  Barring that, we'd like to write everything in Stan itself.

Many of our users don't even use R, so an R-centric solution isn't
general enough for us, though could be helpful in the short run.

One thing Andrew's complained about is that R uses a different notation
(rnorm vs. normal), and has different parameterizations and syntax for
other operations like matrix ops.   (I also think you're missing
a number of draws argument to your rnorm() call if that's meant to be in R).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Continuing sampling
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Continuing sampling
messages.body_plain:
The issue of needing to throw away warmup iterations before
convergence is not at all unique to Stan.

Many MCMC algorithms perform a number of warmup (burnin, adaption,
or whatever you call it) iterations to tune parameters of
the algorithm, then fix the algorithm parameters before converting
to a properly Markovian regime to do sampling.  The reason you
can't keep the warmup iterations is twofold:

1.  they often don't form a Markov chain.  This is true for Stan
and it would also be true of a Metropolis algorithm where you
are estimating the covariance matrix with which to do jumping
proposals and estimating a step size to tune rejection rate.

2.  they typically aren't reasonable draws from the posterior if
you start with random inits far out in the tails.  If you keep
the warmup iterations then you'll bias the final estimates.

I'm not sure what BUGS does for it's adaptive rejection
sampling during warmup --- that is, I don't know if you can
properly use all the draws or if you need to throw away the
warmup draws.  Usually you want to throw away warmup draws
before you've converged to the high mass volume of the
posterior anyway because even though they will wash out
asymptotically, they will bias a small-ish finite sample.

I'm also not sure what JAGS does with its slice sampling, which
can also be adapted.

Some conjugate models don't need to be adapted at all, but
those still suffer from issue (2).

A way to get around issue (1) is to gradually decline adaption
according to something like a Robbins-Monro strategy --- that
can make the result acceptable, but it'll still suffer from
issue (2) if you don't start from a reasonable draw from the
posterior.

- Bob

How do you test if you've achieved convergence?

You can't do the same thing in Stan or any other MCMC that
uses adaptation during burnin/warmup/adaptation, which includes
adaptive Metropolis, for example.

> in this scenario, it's easy to continue sampling if convergence isn't achieved, however the 'warm-up' is a bit more complicated; requiring the following:

>

>

That's what you want to do, though the doubling of N and
M isn't necessary --- you can use any size increase you want.

The convergence test is R-hat, but that won't quite technically
be an "if converged", but rather "if can't reject non-convergence",
which is subtly different --- (split) R-hat being near 1 doesn't guarantee
you've converged.  And it can be especially misleading if you only
run a single chain.

We don't have a way to keep adding more sampling iterations, but will
add that at some point in the future.  But as I said in the last
mail, the savings won't be great.

Subtraction of (x - y) is problematic when either:

 *  x/y is close to 1

 *  x >> y or y >> x

The size of the numbers doesn't matter at all, at least until
you overflow or underflow what a double can represent and
that's not going to happen until some y[n] > 1e100 or y[n] < 1e-100
and then some.

Now we know that E[y^2] >= E[y]^2 in general and we have
to somehow represent that difference, because it's the final
result, so it seems that computing both terms themselves
then subtracting them is more stable than the other way around.

Unless of course, E[y^2] overflows but no (y[n] - E[y])^2
overflows.

Am I missing something critical here?

> E[(y - E[y])^2] is almost always recommended
> but it’s slow as it requires two passed through the data.
> Welford accumulators compute E[(y - E[y])^2] in a
> single pass using clever analytic manipulations.

I agree that the Welford approach is the way to go --- I've
been saying that since long before I worked on Stan!

>
> I understand that a sampling statement such as "Y~foo(a,b)" increments lp__ by foo_log(a,b) minus constant terms,

The constant terms are terms that only involve double values.
So it depends what the arguments are as to what's constant.

> whereas "increment_log_prob(foo_log(Y,a,b)"  increments lp__ by foo_log(a,b) exactly.

Right --- nothing gets dropped there.

> In other word, lp__ is the log-posterior if and only if  there is no sampling statements in the model.
>
> Is this right ?

Almost.  There's also the Jacobians of the inverse transforms for
the constraints.  If you declare a variable

  real<lower=0> x;

then there's a log transform of x in (0,inf) to y = log(x) in (-inf,inf).
That means there's an exp inverse transform back from y in (-inf,inf) to
x = exp(y) in (0,inf).  To adjust for the change of variables,

  log abs( d/dy exp(y)) = y = log(x)

gets added to lp__.

No idea about that one --- it's an RStan issue.

messages.body_plain:
Markov Chain Monte Carlo 101:

In general we contract a Markov chain that generates
a series of states, x_{n}, such that as the number of
states, N, goes to infinity,

lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} 1/N \sum_{n = 0}^{N} f(x_{n})
= \int dx p(x) f(x),

where p(x) is our posterior distribution and f(x) is any
sufficiently nice function.

In practice we’re not interested in the N \rightarrow \infty
limit because we’ll never get there — we want to know
what happens for finite N.  Assuming that the Markov
chain and the posterior distribution play nicely with
each other (a property called geometry ergodicity)
then we have for some large enough but still finite N,

1/N \sum_{n = 0}^{N} f(x_{n}) ~ normal( \int dx p(x) f(x), Var[f] / N).

In words, the Markov chain Monte Carlo estimator,
1/N \sum_{n = 0}^{N} f(x_{n}), is distributed around the
true expectation,  \int dx p(x) f(x), with a variance that
shrinks with the number of samples generated.  We
say that the Markov chain Monte Carlo estimator
_converges in distribution_ towards the true value.

But we can actually do better — although we have the
above property for a Markov chain started at _any_ initial
point, those chains started at points far off in the tails
away from the posterior mass will take a while to reach
the posterior mass.  Those initial samples bias Markov
chain Monte Carlo estimators away from their true values
and we need a pretty large N in order for the rest of
the samples to wash out that initial bias and recover
the convergence above.  But if we simply remove those
initial samples than we can dramatically improve the
precision of our Markov chain Monte Carlo estimator.

Warmup is just the discarding of these initial samples
to yield better estimators.  It’s not necessary, but it
means that we can get better estimators in fewer
samples.  Why call it warmup and not burn in?  Well
burn in has a certain connotation to it — when you
burn a product in you stress test it, throwing away
items that fail and keep the ones that work.  Running
a bunch of Markov chains and then throwing the
ones that fail (get stuck, behave weird, etc) is very,
very bad (with Markov chains, if one chain fails then
they’ve all failed).  Warmup is more evocative of
what’s really going on, which is an equilibration process.

Finally, what’s all this adaptation business about?
The above results all hold for a Markov chain that is
constant — if you start modifying the Markov chain
_while_ generating samples then you lose all of the
precious convergence results.  There are ways of
very carefully modifying Markov chains while maintaining
some results, but they are fragile and hard to implement
and you only get N \rightarrow \infty results, not finite
N results.  Because we discard warmup iterations,
however, we can screw with the Markov chain in that
stage without compromising the validity of the samples
that we keep.

messages.subject: Gaussian Process model for gene expression time-course
messages.subject_clean: Gaussian Process model for gene expression time-course
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan users group,

We are interested in implementing in Stan (through RStan) a Gaussian
Process negative binomial regression model for (RNA-seq) gene expression
time-courses.  The original publication's model is implemented in Matlab
and it runs quite slowly, i.e. it takes > 30 mins per gene and we have
~40K genes in our dataset.  So, we would like to implement this model in
Stan in order to speed it up, and also to improve on the manner in which
differential gene expression is assessed (see below). We would greatly
appreciate the Stan community's help in implementing this model; the
original publication with the model is attached.

As mentioned, an additional concern is how to determine if a gene is
differentially expressed. The original publication used Bayes Factors
between a model in which two conditions or tissues are modeled
separately (H1) and one in which they're modeled together (H0). From
what I've read on the Stan users group, you would probably recommend
using WAIC to compare models, correct?

The original paper used the harmonic mean estimator of the marginal
likelihood, which I know is a terrible estimator. Nevertheless, I
noticed that Stan doesn't implement any path sampling method for
marginal likelihood estimation, so Bayes Factors are not a possibility
in Stan.

For background purposes, we have a well replicated time-course of two
tissues that were sampled every 2 hours for 2 days. The above model is
run on a gene-by-gene basis and then it's determined whether H1 or H0
better fits the data in order to assess differential gene expression.

Any guidance/help would be much appreciated!  ...I've been following the
development of Stan, but haven't yet had time or the need (until now) to
learn how to use it.

Thanks!
Dan Fulop.
--
Daniel Fulop, Ph.D.
Postdoctoral Scholar
Dept. Plant Biology, UC Davis
Maloof Lab, Rm. 2220
Life Sciences Addition, One Shields Ave.
Davis, CA 95616

For even faster inference I would suggest using distributional approximations (Laplace, VB, EP). I recommend LOO-CV with truncated importance sampling instead of WAIC, as it as easy to compute and has a smaller bias in case of surprising observations.
http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_stan.pdf

Aki

messages.body_plain:
The GP model can be simplified substantially by thinking of the
GP are more of a generalized linear model instead of trying to
parameterize the mean and variance.  For example,

Sigma1 <- Covariance matrix for first GP
Sigma 2 <- Covariance matrix for second GP

f1 ~ multi_normal(0, Sigma1);
f2 ~ multi_normal(0, Sigma2);

for (n in 1:n_data)
 y[n] ~ negative_binomial( exp(f1[n]), exp(f2[n]) );

(careful about the parameterizations — this is the overdispersion
parameterization nominally used in in Stan, not the p, r
parameterization).

This kind of data is begging to be fit hierarchically over the genes
(and patients, if measurements were made across a population)
— it would be hard to fit over 40,000 genes but you would get much
better inferences.  In the end you have to figure out wether a simple
but probably biased model that fits over all 40,000 genes is better
or worse than a complex model that fits over few genes but can
incorporate more complexities that arise in the data.  Not something
we can determine a priori, but something you can explore with Stan!

Lastly, if you’re trying to compare modelings using predictive
performance (cross validation, information criteria, etc) then
you have to recognize that you’ve lost the Occam effect in
the marginal likelihood and you won’t have any preference
for the simpler zero-differential model.  One of the immediate
consequences of this is that you can just fit a model with
differential responses and rephrase your question in terms
of an expectation like what is the probability of

P[ | response1 -  response2 | > epsilon ]

for some epsilon (or perhaps a bunch of epsilons).

On Monday, April 13, 2015 at 3:09:17 PM UTC-7, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> The GP model can be simplified substantially by thinking of the

>  y[n] ~ negative_binomial( exp(f1[n]), exp(f2[n]) );

I get the idea of using a finite number of multivariate normals instead of a full Gaussian Process.  We would have to play around with the data to see how many multi_normals we would need.  Thanks for the suggestion!

>
> (careful about the parameterizations — this is the overdispersion
> parameterization nominally used in in Stan, not the p, r
> parameterization).
>
> This kind of data is begging to be fit hierarchically over the genes
> (and patients, if measurements were made across a population)

I know!  I toyed with the idea of asking that in my initial email and decided to leave it out for simplicity's sake and because it's perhaps a bit of a "can of worms."

All genomic scale datasets beg for a joint hierarchical model, but the problem with such models is the heterogeneity in genome scale data.  For instance, some genes have sine-shaped expression time-courses (not necessarily with coinciding peaks and troughs), whereas others have a single peak at a given time of day, and yet others may be roughly invariant throughout the day  ...and others may monotonically decrease or increase through the time-course

Forgive me if I'm wrong, but I think this sort of heterogeneity would require gene clustering as part of the model fitting  ...say with a Dirichlet Process prior or the Gaussian Process approximations of the DPP that I've read about in the Stan list.  One intermediate 2-stage alternative would be to first cluster the genes without "looking" at their expression patterns and then to use a relatively simple hierarchical negative binomial GP to model clusters of covarying genes. This would be practical, though not very Bayesian minded.

...for what it's worth, it's plants and not patients we're dealing with.

> — it would be hard to fit over 40,000 genes but you would get much
> better inferences.  In the end you have to figure out wether a simple
> but probably biased model that fits over all 40,000 genes is better
> or worse than a complex model that fits over few genes but can
> incorporate more complexities that arise in the data.

Given the sort of heterogeneities in time-courses that we know exist in the data, I'd lean towards a somewhat complex hierarchical model or a gene-by-gene approach. What sorts of hierarchical models would you suggest could accommodate this heterogeneity?

>  Not something
> we can determine a priori, but something you can explore with Stan!

I'm happy to explore, but we already know there's a lot of heterogeneity in time-courses.

>
> Lastly, if you’re trying to compare modelings using predictive
> performance (cross validation, information criteria, etc) then
> you have to recognize that you’ve lost the Occam effect in
> the marginal likelihood and you won’t have any preference
> for the simpler zero-differential model.  One of the immediate

> differential responses and rephrase your question in terms
> of an expectation like what is the probability of
>
> P[ | response1 -  response2 | > epsilon ]
>
> for some epsilon (or perhaps a bunch of epsilons).

>
> I get the idea of using a finite number of multivariate normals instead of a full Gaussian Process.  We would have to play around with the data to see how many multi_normals we would need.  Thanks for the suggestion!

Oh, I was just suggesting the more direct

mu[n] = exp(f1[n])

instead of the

mu[n] = exp(f1[n]) / ( exp(f1[n]) + sigma[n] )

used in the paper (or whatever the right equation is — I’m going off the top of my head).

The multivariate normal is how you implement _any_ GP in practice,
it’s just particularly transparent in Stan.

> I know!  I toyed with the idea of asking that in my initial email and decided to leave it out for simplicity's sake and because it's perhaps a bit of a "can of worms."
>
> All genomic scale datasets beg for a joint hierarchical model, but the problem with such models is the heterogeneity in genome scale data.  For instance, some genes have sine-shaped expression time-courses (not necessarily with coinciding peaks and troughs), whereas others have a single peak at a given time of day, and yet others may be roughly invariant throughout the day  ...and others may monotonically decrease or increase through the time-course
>
> Forgive me if I'm wrong, but I think this sort of heterogeneity would require gene clustering as part of the model fitting  ...say with a Dirichlet Process prior or the Gaussian Process approximations of the DPP that I've read about in the Stan list.  One intermediate 2-stage alternative would be to first cluster the genes without "looking" at their expression patterns and then to use a relatively simple hierarchical negative binomial GP to model clusters of covarying genes. This would be practical, though not very Bayesian minded.
>
> ...for what it's worth, it's plants and not patients we're dealing with.

> Given the sort of heterogeneities in time-courses that we know exist in the data, I'd lean towards a somewhat complex hierarchical model or a gene-by-gene approach. What sorts of hierarchical models would you suggest could accommodate this heterogeneity?

There’s a lot that can be done before resorting to Dirichlet processes!
One of the approaches we strongly recommend is to start simple and
add structure in stages.

So start with a small number of genes and fit everything independently
to gauge your computational budget.  Then you can consider very
simple hierarchical models, for example, making the length scale of
the GP hyperparameters hierarchical across each individual gene.
Adding more layers to the hierarchy, to take into account the varying
time-responses you note, can be considered much later on.

Personally I would put a little more thought into the measurement
model — if the measurement of gene expression is correlated then
any model that tries to measure differential expression while ignoring
the correlation will yield misleading results!  This is especially
important if any of that heterogeneity comes from environmental
factors that can be incorporated into the measurement model.

> Thanks for suggesting this!  I rather like this idea.  I'll ask for feedback about reasonable epsilon values when the time comes.

There won’t be any particular value of epsilon — you’ll have to explore
the model and come up with some bespoke narrative appropriate to
the journal/funding agency/community.  For example, consider plotting
the probability as a function of epsilon using the shape of the function
to construct a narrative.

> On Apr 14, 2015, at 2:38 AM, Linas Mockus <linasm...@gmail.com> wrote:

>
> The problem I am having is solving several models in stan.  There are two independent data sets Y1=model1(x,theta1)+eps1 and Y2=model2(x,theta1,theta2)+eps2 where both eps1 and eps2 are normal. One way is to solve both models simultaneously in stan.  However, it might be easier to estimate theta1 for the first data set Y1 in stan, approximate theta1 estimates via normal in R, transfer means and sigmas of theta1 to a different stan code which estimates theta2 using the second data set Y2 and means/sigmas for theta1.  Is this approach reasonable.

I don't think so.  What would happen is that you'd be using the
*approximate* posterior for theta1 in model1 as a prior for model2
if I understand you correctly.

> Currently I have stan code to estimate theta1 and theta2 simultaneously (basically by having one loop for the first data set (m_SR) and another loop for the second data set (m).

This is actually a coherent model to estimate theta1 and theta2 jointly,
where theta1 is a paramter of both models.

It would also make sense to estimate the two models independently from
scratch.

- Bob

One way is to solve both models simultaneously in stan.  However, it might be easier to estimate theta1 for the first data set Y1 in stan, approximate theta1 estimates via normal in R, transfer means and sigmas of theta1 to a different stan code which estimates theta2 using the second data set Y2 and means/sigmas for theta1. > This is actually a coherent model to estimate theta1 and theta2 jointly,
> where theta1 is a paramter of both models.
>
> It would also make sense to estimate the two models independently from
> scratch.
>
> - Bob
