messages.subject: Re: Gaussian Process model for gene expression time-course
messages.subject_clean: Gaussian Process model for gene expression time-course
messages.body_plain:
I mentioned about this to Harri Lähdesmäki (we are soon in the same department) and he told that they now have also Stan implementation. Harri asked Tarmo Äijö to post the model here after checking that everything is ok.

Aki

On Monday, April 13, 2015 at 6:45:41 PM UTC+3, Daniel Fulop wrote:

> Dear Stan users group,
>
> We are interested in implementing in Stan (through RStan) a Gaussian
> Process negative binomial regression model for (RNA-seq) gene expression
> time-courses.  The original publication's model is implemented in Matlab
> and it runs quite slowly, i.e. it takes > 30 mins per gene and we have
> ~40K genes in our dataset.  So, we would like to implement this model in
> Stan in order to speed it up, and also to improve on the manner in which
> differential gene expression is assessed (see below). We would greatly
> appreciate the Stan community's help in implementing this model; the
> original publication with the model is attached.
>
> As mentioned, an additional concern is how to determine if a gene is
> differentially expressed. The original publication used Bayes Factors
> between a model in which two conditions or tissues are modeled
> separately (H1) and one in which they're modeled together (H0). From
> what I've read on the Stan users group, you would probably recommend
> using WAIC to compare models, correct?
>
> The original paper used the harmonic mean estimator of the marginal
> likelihood, which I know is a terrible estimator. Nevertheless, I
> noticed that Stan doesn't implement any path sampling method for
> marginal likelihood estimation, so Bayes Factors are not a possibility
> in Stan.
>
> For background purposes, we have a well replicated time-course of two
> tissues that were sampled every 2 hours for 2 days. The above model is
> run on a gene-by-gene basis and then it's determined whether H1 or H0
> better fits the data in order to assess differential gene expression.
>
> Any guidance/help would be much appreciated!  ...I've been following the
> development of Stan, but haven't yet had time or the need (until now) to
> learn how to use it.
>
> Thanks!
> Dan Fulop.
> --
> Daniel Fulop, Ph.D.
> Postdoctoral Scholar
> Dept. Plant Biology, UC Davis
> Maloof Lab, Rm. 2220
> Life Sciences Addition, One Shields Ave.
> Davis, CA 95616
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Gaussian Process model for gene expression time-course
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Gaussian Process model for gene expression time-course
messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael,

Michael Betancourt wrote:
> >
> > I get the idea of using a finite number of multivariate normals instead of a full Gaussian Process.  We would have to play around with the data to see how many multi_normals we would need.  Thanks for the suggestion!
>
> Oh, I was just suggesting the more direct
>
> mu[n] = exp(f1[n])
>
> instead of the
>
> mu[n] = exp(f1[n]) / ( exp(f1[n]) + sigma[n] )
>
> used in the paper (or whatever the right equation is — I’m going off the top of my head).
>
> The multivariate normal is how you implement _any_ GP in practice,
> it’s just particularly transparent in Stan.

Okay, got it.

>
> > I know!  I toyed with the idea of asking that in my initial email and decided to leave it out for simplicity's sake and because it's perhaps a bit of a "can of worms."
> >
> > All genomic scale datasets beg for a joint hierarchical model, but the problem with such models is the heterogeneity in genome scale data.  For instance, some genes have sine-shaped expression time-courses (not necessarily with coinciding peaks and troughs), whereas others have a single peak at a given time of day, and yet others may be roughly invariant throughout the day  ...and others may monotonically decrease or increase through the time-course
> >
> > Forgive me if I'm wrong, but I think this sort of heterogeneity would require gene clustering as part of the model fitting  ...say with a Dirichlet Process prior or the Gaussian Process approximations of the DPP that I've read about in the Stan list.  One intermediate 2-stage alternative would be to first cluster the genes without "looking" at their expression patterns and then to use a relatively simple hierarchical negative binomial GP to model clusters of covarying genes. This would be practical, though not very Bayesian minded.
> >
> > ...for what it's worth, it's plants and not patients we're dealing with.
>
> > Given the sort of heterogeneities in time-courses that we know exist in the data, I'd lean towards a somewhat complex hierarchical model or a gene-by-gene approach. What sorts of hierarchical models would you suggest could accommodate this heterogeneity?
>
> There’s a lot that can be done before resorting to Dirichlet processes!
> One of the approaches we strongly recommend is to start simple and
> add structure in stages.

Okay, pardon my ignorance. Certainly the NB dispersion is typically modeled hierarchically in RNAseq differential expression methods, although almost always in an empirical bayes fashion.  So, that could be modeled hierarchically for all genes; the assumption typically is that genes whose mean expression levels are similar have similar dispersion, so it's a mean-variance relationship that's modeled.

The function ShrinkSeq() (which is part of the ShrinkBayes) package implements a variety of RNAseq models that are more complex than that of other RNAseq software. ShrinkSeq isn't meant for time courses, but we could borrow some ideas from it. They hierarchically model several additional aspects apart from the dispersion, such as incorporating random effects (i.e. NB-GLMM) for experimental design variables (I suppose this sort of thing is what you are alluding to with regards to measurement error).

As to measurement error, I just spoke to Hagop (who actually did the tissue sampling and lab work) and the sampling was "pseudo-random" spatially (i.e. not planned but not confounded with spacial plant placement), but no spatial information was recorded.  So, such information cannot be used to inform the model.  However, the plant field was relatively small (just 2 rows), etc.

One measurement error aspect that could be taken into account , though, is the sampling day.  Hagop has 3 replicates per time point per tissue, and 2 whole days of samples; all 3 replicates were sampled (i.e. frozen in liquid nitrogen) within ~10 minutes of each other .  So, we are planning to "collapse" both days to increase the time point replication to 6.  Conceivably sampling day could be assumed to influence the time-varying component of the model (not the heterogeneity of the time-course pattern, but rather the relative developmental acceleration/deceleration  ...i.e. the differential timing of cell maturation in the original paper); at least it's worth experimenting with such a specification.

>
> So start with a small number of genes and fit everything independently
> to gauge your computational budget.  Then you can consider very
> simple hierarchical models, for example, making the length scale of
> the GP hyperparameters hierarchical across each individual gene

What do you mean by the length scale?  What I'm gathering is that we would model the number of MVNs that make up the GP hierarchically so that there's a common distribution for all genes as to the number of MVNs, but then each gene would sample its MVN number from this common distribution.

> .
> Adding more layers to the hierarchy, to take into account the varying
> time-responses you note, can be considered much later on.

That may not be necessary.  I think we can leave each gene to have its own time-varying response.  Otherwise we would need something like a DPP for that aspect of the model, I think.

>
> Personally I would put a little more thought into the measurement
> model — if the measurement of gene expression is correlated

What do you mean by correlated?  To what?

> then
> any model that tries to measure differential expression while ignoring
> the correlation will yield misleading results!  This is especially
> important if any of that heterogeneity comes from environmental
> factors that can be incorporated into the measurement model.

As I said, the plant field was relatively small, and Hagop didn't keep track of the spatial sampling.  I would say that the environmental heterogeneity factors are relatively well controlled.

>
> > Thanks for suggesting this!  I rather like this idea.  I'll ask for feedback about reasonable epsilon values when the time comes.
>
> There won’t be any particular value of epsilon — you’ll have to explore
> the model and come up with some bespoke narrative appropriate to
> the journal/funding agency/community.  For example, consider plotting
> the probability as a function of epsilon using the shape of the function
> to construct a narrative.

Okay.  I had gotten then idea initially, but this further suggestion is quite informative.

We'll wait for Harri and Tarmo to post their Stan code and work from there to add hierarchical layers, etc.

Thanks,
Dan.
>

> On Apr 15, 2015, at 4:11 AM, Lionel Henry <lione...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> That said, I agree it would be great if Stan had natively the
> ability to use previously sampled draws. Rather than a hack where
> the draws are used as data inputs, it may make sense for Stan to
> take explicitely such a sample as input to use one draw at each
> step.

We spent most of the Stan meeting yesterday talking about just
this feature, which Andrew really wants.  Here's the summary of
what we want to do:

  * write a generated quantities block, and
  * evaluate it AFTER the samples are drawn from Stan

so that the results are the same as if it had been originally
included in the Stan program.

That way, you can play with different generated quanitities
computations without having to fiddle indexes the way you
have to do with extracted draws in RStan at the moment.

I think it's doable, but no idea when we'll get to it.
The major stumbling block now is the ability to read the
output CSV file back into structured inputs.  If we could do
that, all we'd need to do is write the C++ code and figure
out how to plumb it through all the interfaces.

> This could be used to perform simulations with r.v. parameters,
> but I wonder if it could also be used in model fitting to account
> for the uncertainty of previously estimated parameters, such as
> multiple imputations. Would HMC behave well with this scheme?

We don't know --- it's an open research area related to
Michael's adiabatic sampling.

It's also somewhat related to the notion of cut() that our
friends in pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics want us to apply
in a BUGS-like fashion in the situation where they trust
their PK model but know their PD model is misspecified and
don't want the misspecified model distorting the well estimated
PK model that still has uncertainty.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
> On Apr 15, 2015, at 3:33 AM, Daniel Fulop <dfulo...@gmail.com> wrote:
...

> Okay, pardon my ignorance. Certainly the NB dispersion is typically modeled hierarchically in RNAseq differential expression methods, although almost always in an empirical bayes fashion.

Right --- there's Brad Efron's whole recent book.  It's
what we'd call "maximum marginal likelihood" because Andrew
doesn't like "empirical Bayes" because of the connotation that
other Bayesian approaches aren't empirical.

Of course, we'd much rather do full Bayes and Stan's powerful enough to
do whole-genome modeling of this kind of differential expression
data.

> So, that could be modeled hierarchically for all genes; the assumption typically is that genes whose mean expression levels are similar have similar dispersion, so it's a mean-variance relationship that's modeled.

My understanding was that this didn't work very well and that there
was a huge amount of inter-experimental variation that wasn't accounted
for by a simple mean-variance relationship within or across experiments.

> The function ShrinkSeq() (which is part of the ShrinkBayes) package implements a variety of RNAseq models that are more complex than that of other RNAseq software. ShrinkSeq isn't meant for time courses, but we could borrow some ideas from it. They hierarchically model several additional aspects apart from the dispersion, such as incorporating random effects (i.e. NB-GLMM) for experimental design variables (I suppose this sort of thing is what you are alluding to with regards to measurement error).
>
> As to measurement error, I just spoke to Hagop (who actually did the tissue sampling and lab work) and the sampling was "pseudo-random" spatially (i.e. not planned but not confounded with spacial plant placement), but no spatial information was recorded.  So, such information cannot be used to inform the model.  However, the plant field was relatively small (just 2 rows), etc.
>
> One measurement error aspect that could be taken into account , though, is the sampling day.

I'd also think you could take the basic sequencing data measurement into
account as well as the replication process that precedes it, which I believe
also has a huge amount of "lab hands" related variation, which is one of
the things that makes replication in this field so difficult.

>  Hagop has 3 replicates per time point per tissue, and 2 whole days of samples; all 3 replicates were sampled (i.e. frozen in liquid nitrogen) within ~10 minutes of each other .  So, we are planning to "collapse" both days to increase the time point replication to 6.  Conceivably sampling day could be assumed to influence the time-varying component of the model (not the heterogeneity of the time-course pattern, but rather the relative developmental acceleration/deceleration  ...i.e. the differential timing of cell maturation in the original paper); at least it's worth experimenting with such a specification.

I've seen some really neat work on circadian rhythm type analysis
out of Broad, where the same tissue is repeatedly sequenced over the
course of 24 hours or more (mainly with fruit flies in what I've seen).

>> So start with a small number of genes and fit everything independently
>> to gauge your computational budget.  Then you can consider very
>> simple hierarchical models, for example, making the length scale of
>> the GP hyperparameters hierarchical across each individual gene
> What do you mean by the length scale?  What I'm gathering is that we would model the number of MVNs that make up the GP hierarchically so that there's a common distribution for all genes as to the number of MVNs, but then each gene would sample its MVN number from this common distribution.

The length scale is a typical scale parameter --- it's in the
denominator of the squared exponential covariance matrix construction.
It controls how much the fitted function is allowed to wiggle --- that
is, how distance affects covariance.

>> .
>> Adding more layers to the hierarchy, to take into account the varying
>> time-responses you note, can be considered much later on.
> That may not be necessary.  I think we can leave each gene to have its own time-varying response.  Otherwise we would need something like a DPP for that aspect of the model, I think.

I don't think it'd need a DP, but then I'd also suggest starting
simple and seeing where the simple model doesn't fit using posterior
predictive checking.

>> Personally I would put a little more thought into the measurement
>> model — if the measurement of gene expression is correlated
> What do you mean by correlated?  To what?

I'm guessing among the genes.  At least that kind of co-expression is what
a lot of people are looking for to induce metabolic pathways.  I
don't know how many genes your plants have, but we can't really scale
to a 40K x 40K correlation matrix!  So what I've seen people do is try
to build something like "topic" models --- latent effects that account
for correlations in an implicitly low-rank sort of way.

And please keep us updated --- my wife used to work in this area and
I've been dying to do some work on gene expression measurement and
pathway induction.  But I think I'll only have time to soak it up by proxy.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Gaussian Process model for gene expression time-course
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Gaussian Process model for gene expression time-course
messages.body_plain:
>
> Okay, pardon my ignorance. Certainly the NB dispersion is typically modeled hierarchically in RNAseq differential expression methods, although almost always in an empirical bayes fashion.  So, that could be modeled hierarchically for all genes; the assumption typically is that genes whose mean expression levels are similar have similar dispersion, so it's a mean-variance relationship that's modeled.
>
> The function ShrinkSeq() (which is part of the ShrinkBayes) package implements a variety of RNAseq models that are more complex than that of other RNAseq software. ShrinkSeq isn't meant for time courses, but we could borrow some ideas from it. They hierarchically model several additional aspects apart from the dispersion, such as incorporating random effects (i.e. NB-GLMM) for experimental design variables (I suppose this sort of thing is what you are alluding to with regards to measurement error).
>
> As to measurement error, I just spoke to Hagop (who actually did the tissue sampling and lab work) and the sampling was "pseudo-random" spatially (i.e. not planned but not confounded with spacial plant placement), but no spatial information was recorded.  So, such information cannot be used to inform the model.  However, the plant field was relatively small (just 2 rows), etc.

"i.e. not planned but not confounded with spacial plant placement”
I understand the realities of the lab environment and appreciate
the candor, but statements like this make reproducibility supporters
cry a single tear at night.  ;-)

> One measurement error aspect that could be taken into account , though, is the sampling day.  Hagop has 3 replicates per time point per tissue, and 2 whole days of samples; all 3 replicates were sampled (i.e. frozen in liquid nitrogen) within ~10 minutes of each other .  So, we are planning to "collapse" both days to increase the time point replication to 6.  Conceivably sampling day could be assumed to influence the time-varying component of the model (not the heterogeneity of the time-course pattern, but rather the relative developmental acceleration/deceleration  ...i.e. the differential timing of cell maturation in the original paper); at least it's worth experimenting with such a specification.

Yeah, a huge benefit of hierarchical modeling is that you don’t have
to “collapse” your data to try to improve statistical power.

By measurement process I literally meant the physical process
that takes gene expression to some discrete counts on a computer.
Things like PCR, for example, confound different gene expressions
when trying to deconvolve the individual components and induce
nontrivial correlations in the measured data that is often ignored.
Reducing the entire measurement to “genes express proteins,
proteins magically turn into NB responses” is hugely simplified —
it may be sufficient for a given analysis but you have to be
prepared to argue that.

We have lots of practice in finding flaws in oversimplified models...

> What do you mean by the length scale?  What I'm gathering is that we would model the number of MVNs that make up the GP hierarchically so that there's a common distribution for all genes as to the number of MVNs, but then each gene would sample its MVN number from this common distribution.

I’m referring to the hyperparameters of the GP.  If you have the
heterogeneity in time responses that you claim (some increase,
some oscillate, some are constant, etc) then building a hierarchical
GP with common hyperparameters will not give you a good fit!

Really want you want to do is group the different time responses
and fit each individual group with an appropriate GP, perhaps
with the hyper parameters of those groups in a global hierarchy
themselves.

> That may not be necessary.  I think we can leave each gene to have its own time-varying response.  Otherwise we would need something like a DPP for that aspect of the model, I think.

Again, there are a million things to do before looking at DPPs.
Even crude clustering combined with static hierarchical modeling
on those clusters can be hugely powerful, but you’ll have to spend
time informing those clusters using prior knowledge from experiment
and theory.  Good inferences don’t come cheap.

Anyways, start simple (say a hierarchy over each gene individually,
whether the hierarchy is over GPs or GP hyper parameters) and
build from there, incorporating time or spatial effects or clustering
the genes, etc.  Of course we’re happy to help in that process,
and a side benefit of starting simple is that it makes it easier for
us to understand your scientific motivations without having the
necessary background.

messages.subject: blending Stan with interfaces
messages.subject_clean: blending Stan with interfaces
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Following on the discussion on "testify" which resulted in a planned delayed generated quantitiy block as far as I understood. Here is why I think you could reconsider this more in a direction of "testify":

Quite a number of scientific software is written as a mix of languages, i.e. a very successfull model is to code most of data handling/fiddling/processing/whatever thing in something "light" like R or Python. Then the hard stuff should always be done in something like C++. At least this is how I have done much of my research. Following this approach means that Stan should opt to make possibly all those tremendous functionality in Stan not only available in those few blocks, but rather it should be the goal to bridge Stan space with the interface space.

This is a bit contrary to the current approach "keep the interfaces lean and let the C++ Stan handle" - but only in some sense. What would be awesome to have at some point is to tie all those Stan function into the interfaces you have, i.e. I would find it extremely helpful to just straight be abel to call lkj densities from R. Of course, not all interfaces are as rich as others, but then languages like R are so powerful that not making use of this would be a pitty. Just an example, with the current testify stuff I can define a Stan functions, which, say, takes the two parameters a and b as argument. Then having the function in R space allows me to do stuff like

testify("model.stan") which has "real calc_stuff(real a, real b) {}"

# also assume we have a fit

post <- extract(fit, c("a", "b"))

do.call(Vectorize(calc_stuff), post)

Now, the last call is likely awkward looking for anyone not programming R for a while, but it is a nice example of how easy some things are in R, i.e. I get almost for free a mechanism to do posterior simulations in a very straightforward way.

And one more argument for blending Stan into the interfaces - each of us is best in commanding with the interfaces the objects we care about. Hence, fitting Stan tightly into the user environment is a huge step.

I am speaking here as a user, of course. Software wise, I think there are approaches as Swig which goes beyond R (for R we have the wonderful Rcpp) which may we worth to consider.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject_clean: Current ODE solver limitations and potential future capacities
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Many thanks for putting so much effort into developing Stan - I feel like my models are running twice as fast now compared to last year!

Also, thanks for putting in the ODE solver - I implemented the sho example and it's great fun, but I have a couple of questions:

1) It seems as if the ODE solver requires that all observations are sequential, i.e that no two observations where taken at the same time.
Is this correct, and if so, is this a temporary or permanent limitation? And would adding a bit of "jiggle" to observations be a sensible way of going around this,
i.e  adjusting  observation times from (1,1,1) to (1-eps,1,1+eps)?

2) It says in the documentation that observation times must be fixed and taken from data. I presume that this means that it is impossible to fit a model where the measurements are taken with an unknown lag/incubation time? I.e. observation recorded at some time T, but measurement/response occurring at time T-delta, delta being a random variable (and fitted within stan) ?
Is the "fixed-time" requirement a permanent feature of the ODE solver, or something that might change in the (near) future?

Best regards,
Gustaf

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Current ODE solver limitations and potential future capacities
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gustaf,

On Thu, Apr 16, 2015 at 5:17 PM Gustaf Rydevik <gustaf....@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi,
>
> Many thanks for putting so much effort into developing Stan - I feel like my models are running twice as fast now compared to last year!

That's great. Make sure you're looking at the number of effective sample sizes.

> Also, thanks for putting in the ODE solver - I implemented the sho example and it's great fun, but I have a couple of questions:
>
> 1) It seems as if the ODE solver requires that all observations are sequential, i.e that no two observations where taken at the same time.
> Is this correct, and if so, is this a temporary or permanent limitation? And would adding a bit of "jiggle" to observations be a sensible way of going around this,
> i.e  adjusting  observation times from (1,1,1) to (1-eps,1,1+eps)?

It's a limitation of the current solver we're using, Boost. Nothing in Stan is set is stone, but I don't see us relaxing this anytime soon. What in the model would require times to be identical?

I see wanting to start the initial time at the same time as the first data point (see issue 1340 https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1340), but I haven't seen enough models that providing multiple time points is the right thing to do. If you have a concrete example, that would be interesting to see.

> 2) It says in the documentation that observation times must be fixed and taken from data. I presume that this means that it is impossible to fit a model where the measurements are taken with an unknown lag/incubation time? I.e. observation recorded at some time T, but measurement/response occurring at time T-delta, delta being a random variable (and fitted within stan) ?
> Is the "fixed-time" requirement a permanent feature of the ODE solver, or something that might change in the (near) future?

Yes, time being forced as data will be permanent. One of the other devs (i.e. Michael) might chime in and say otherwise, but I think the problem gets a lot harder when you allow time to be a parameter. (And it's plenty hard now.)

Fortunately, the initial state can be a parameter and the ode function can be written as a function with a lag, so all is not lost. We just won't allow the time itself to be declared as a parameter.

messages.body_plain:
Right now, that's being done in the interfaces, so the
issue tracker for RStan is where to make that request:

 https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/issues

It's much better to put things there where they can be
tracked in one place than into e-mail where it'll get
lost.

It should actually be reasonably easy if the estimate is just assuming
the remaining iterations will take the same average time as the ones
that have happened.  That'll almost certainly underestimate time after
10 iterations (the first few iterations are usually fast) and then
pretty quickly move to overestimating because warmup iterations are usually
slower.

We can roll it into a general feature for Stan 3 updates
on the C++ side.  It all has to get pushed to and from
the interfaces, though, so it's a bit of work in how it'll
all be formatted, etc.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am running a model that requires the cdf of a gamma distribution:

gamma_cdf_log(threshold,dose[j,h]/scale,1/scale);

When I run with gamma_cdf I get an overflow error, which is not suprising as I had the same problem when I previously implemented the model in C++. However, I also get the same error when I run with gamma_log_cdf:

Error in function boost::math::tgamma<e>(e): Result of tgamma is too large to represent.

I was under the impression that gamma_log_cdf should use lgamma instead of tgamma, or at least that is what my C++ code does.

Any help would be appreciated.

Chris Steele

log(1 - CDF).  There's already an issue to fix these,
but it's not on our short-term to-do list.

One thing you can do is try to constrain whichever parameter
is causing a problem.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Current ODE solver limitations and potential future capacities
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Current ODE solver limitations and potential future capacities
messages.body_plain:
> On Apr 17, 2015, at 8:56 AM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
>
> Hi Gustaf,
>
> On Thu, Apr 16, 2015 at 5:17 PM Gustaf Rydevik <gustaf....@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi,
>
> Many thanks for putting so much effort into developing Stan - I feel like my models are running twice as fast now compared to last year!
>
> That's great. Make sure you're looking at the number of effective sample sizes.
>
>
> Also, thanks for putting in the ODE solver - I implemented the sho example and it's great fun, but I have a couple of questions:
>
> 1) It seems as if the ODE solver requires that all observations are sequential, i.e that no two observations where taken at the same time.
> Is this correct, and if so, is this a temporary or permanent limitation? And would adding a bit of "jiggle" to observations be a sensible way of going around this,
> i.e  adjusting  observation times from (1,1,1) to (1-eps,1,1+eps)?
>
> It's a limitation of the current solver we're using, Boost. Nothing in Stan is set is stone, but I don't see us relaxing this anytime soon. What in the model would require times to be identical?
>
> I see wanting to start the initial time at the same time as the first data point (see issue 1340 https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1340), but I haven't seen enough models that providing multiple time points is the right thing to do. If you have a concrete example, that would be interesting to see.

You could jitter a bit if there are multiple observations of the same thing at the same time.

> 2) It says in the documentation that observation times must be fixed and taken from data. I presume that this means that it is impossible to fit a model where the measurements are taken with an unknown lag/incubation time? I.e. observation recorded at some time T, but measurement/response occurring at time T-delta, delta being a random variable (and fitted within stan) ?
> Is the "fixed-time" requirement a permanent feature of the ODE solver, or something that might change in the (near) future?
>
> Yes, time being forced as data will be permanent. One of the other devs (i.e. Michael) might chime in and say otherwise, but I think the problem gets a lot harder when you allow time to be a parameter. (And it's plenty hard now.)
>
> Fortunately, the initial state can be a parameter and the ode function can be written as a function with a lag, so all is not lost. We just won't allow the time itself to be declared as a parameter.

Exactly --- the diff eq depends on time (data, not parameter) and
also arbitrary parameters, which you can then combine any way you want
in the system diff eq function.

Is it the time of observation that's uncertain or the time of
some effect?  If it's the latter, it makes more sense to put it
in the system anyway.  I'm not sure how people write these in general,
but you're not the first person to bring that up.

We can't have the times be uncertain because those are the points at
which the diff eq gets solved and we don't have derivative information there.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Current ODE solver limitations and potential future capacities
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Current ODE solver limitations and potential future capacities
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

If your data set has time-points which are the same, then a simple (but tedious) solution would be to stop the integrator each time you have a doublicated time-point in your data and then restart with the last state you got at the next suitable time-point. This could be done in principle by Stan for for the user and this would be really great to have, i.e. a Stan function which stops and starts the ODE solver

- at equal time points
- whenever an event (dosing) occurs

i.e. this would be a convenience function which wraps around the current ODE solver. Since ODEs have the nice property that you can stop and restart at any time, this easy in principle but hard to get it right (carry forward initial state, etc.).

Best,
Sebastian

underflow of derivatives when you have log CDFs, because in the
tails you wind up dividing by the (non-log) CDF.

then you should just be able to pass in double values if you just
want to test behavior.

It's a little trickier if you want to also evaluate gradients.
Then you either need to use our functionals and create an appropriately
functor or use the library directly.

You can also see derivative behavior by using finite differences on
an implementation you trust.

messages.body_plain:
Everything's header only in Stan's C++, so it's just a matter
of getting the right includes.  If STAN_HOME is where Stan
is installed, then the libraries you need are here

  EIGEN_HOME = $(STAN_HOME)/lib/eigen_3.2.4
  BOOST_HOME = $(STAN_HOME)/lib/boost_1.55.0

and the paths to include are

  -I. -I$(STAN_HOME)/src -I$(BOOST_HOME) -I$(EIGEN_HOME)

We don't have any user-facing doc for the C++ API.  It sort
of starts from the makefiles and the unit-test files.  Running
through the unit tests would be anotehr alternative. They run
from a top-level python script which includes its own doc.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Current ODE solver limitations and potential future capacities
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Current ODE solver limitations and potential future capacities
messages.body_plain:
Hi Daniel, Bob and Sebastian,

Thanks  for your answers!

I'm playing around with fitting antibody and nucleic acid kinetic curves to experimental infection data using Lotka-Volterra equations (and I'll make a separate post on my troubles there). In these kinds of studies, observations are often done at regular intervals, e.g. day 1,2,5,10 and 20 post infection for a number of individuals; thus the wish to have multiple observations at the same time point. But it sounds like either jiggling, or just averaging the observations for each timepoint beforehand, would be decent workaround.

If such data are collected in an observational study, there might be an unknown incubation time before symptoms start showing, and so we would have some uncertainty in how long along the kinetic curve we were - but the suggestion of having a "lag" parameter in the diffeq function sounds promising, and I'll give that a go if and when I get far enough to start modelling incubation times.

Best,
Gustaf

On Friday, April 17, 2015 at 7:42:52 AM UTC+1, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> Hi!
>
> If your data set has time-points which are the same, then a simple (but tedious) solution would be to stop the integrator each time you have a doublicated time-point in your data and then restart with the last state you got at the next suitable time-point. This could be done in principle by Stan for for the user and this would be really great to have, i.e. a Stan function which stops and starts the ODE solver
>
> - at equal time points
> - whenever an event (dosing) occurs
>
> i.e. this would be a convenience function which wraps around the current ODE solver. Since ODEs have the nice property that you can stop and restart at any time, this easy in principle but hard to get it right (carry forward initial state, etc.).
>
> Best,
> Sebastian
>
>
> On Friday, April 17, 2015 at 7:27:03 AM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >
> > > On Apr 17, 2015, at 8:56 AM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
> > >
> > > Hi Gustaf,
> > >
> > > On Thu, Apr 16, 2015 at 5:17 PM Gustaf Rydevik <gustaf....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Hi,
> > >
> > > Many thanks for putting so much effort into developing Stan - I feel like my models are running twice as fast now compared to last year!
> > >
> > > That's great. Make sure you're looking at the number of effective sample sizes.
> > >
> > >
> > > Also, thanks for putting in the ODE solver - I implemented the sho example and it's great fun, but I have a couple of questions:
> > >
> > > 1) It seems as if the ODE solver requires that all observations are sequential, i.e that no two observations where taken at the same time.
> > > Is this correct, and if so, is this a temporary or permanent limitation? And would adding a bit of "jiggle" to observations be a sensible way of going around this,
> > > i.e  adjusting  observation times from (1,1,1) to (1-eps,1,1+eps)?
> > >
> > > It's a limitation of the current solver we're using, Boost. Nothing in Stan is set is stone, but I don't see us relaxing this anytime soon. What in the model would require times to be identical?
> > >
> > > I see wanting to start the initial time at the same time as the first data point (see issue 1340 https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1340), but I haven't seen enough models that providing multiple time points is the right thing to do. If you have a concrete example, that would be interesting to see.
> >
> > You could jitter a bit if there are multiple observations of the same thing at the same time.
> >
> > > 2) It says in the documentation that observation times must be fixed and taken from data. I presume that this means that it is impossible to fit a model where the measurements are taken with an unknown lag/incubation time? I.e. observation recorded at some time T, but measurement/response occurring at time T-delta, delta being a random variable (and fitted within stan) ?
> > > Is the "fixed-time" requirement a permanent feature of the ODE solver, or something that might change in the (near) future?
> > >
> > > Yes, time being forced as data will be permanent. One of the other devs (i.e. Michael) might chime in and say otherwise, but I think the problem gets a lot harder when you allow time to be a parameter. (And it's plenty hard now.)
> > >
> > > Fortunately, the initial state can be a parameter and the ode function can be written as a function with a lag, so all is not lost. We just won't allow the time itself to be declared as a parameter.
> >
> > Exactly --- the diff eq depends on time (data, not parameter) and
> > also arbitrary parameters, which you can then combine any way you want
> > in the system diff eq function.
> >
> > Is it the time of observation that's uncertain or the time of
> > some effect?  If it's the latter, it makes more sense to put it
> > in the system anyway.  I'm not sure how people write these in general,
> > but you're not the first person to bring that up.
> >
> > We can't have the times be uncertain because those are the points at
> > which the diff eq gets solved and we don't have derivative information there.
> >
> > - Bob
> >

another solution is to run the ODE integrator through the unique set of time-values and later on with some index-fiddling associate the predicted mean value at the time point when you have multiple observations to the same ODE result.

messages.body_plain:
Are you aggregating the individuals somehow?

I'd think that even if you had multiple measurements, you'd
be assuming the diff eq solution would be the same.
That is, y would have K measurements for each time t in (1:T).

  data {
    vector[K] y[T];
    ...
  }

Then the model has a single solution y_hat giving you expected
individual behavior, then you add noisy measurements (and unexplained
inter-individual variance):

  model {

    y_hat ~ integrate_ode(...);

    for (t in 1:T)
      y[t] ~ normal(y_hat[t], sigma_y);
    ...
  }

- Bob

I am asking, because I burned myself once with a model where I forgot to put a prior on some parameter which did not end up in the likelihood for some reasons... this killed NUTS; but I take that as long as a sensible prior is in place all is good.
>
> Right, that makes sense since then the posterior is improper and that one parameter would not meet the conditions for a U-turn...

The posterior has to be proper or NUTS will run with the
impropriety.

I just meant in my response that an extra normal(0,1) variable
will absolutely not kill the NUTS condition and not slow things
down overall very much.

> I recall there's some parameter that limits the maximum number of steps but not what it's called.

That just masks the problem.  Whenver you bump up against the limit, either
the model needs to be fixed or the limit needs to be extended.  It's there
so Stan doesn't just hang on the first go-round.

>  If the prior is normal(0,sigma) (i.e. the parameter is an unused random effect level) you could get the funnel posterior and have a similar problem, but only if sigma is estimated to be large...  and that's where my intuition for this runs out.

This isn't relevant if you have a fixed normal(0,1) prior,
or even if it's a hierarchical prior that's well constrained.

The problem with the funnel is the curvature issue --- with
high hyperprior variance, the posterior is flat, whereas with
low hyperprior variance, the posterior is very sharply curved.
So you can't get a mass matrix and step-size that work everywhere.

The manual covers both these cases in the problematic posterior
and reparameterization chapters.

- Bob

If I plot the HMC chain of sampled (1,1)-entries of the cholesky factor of a correlation matrix, they remain constant at one.

Question 1: Is this expected?

I am under the impression that this is indeed expected. My reasoning goes as follows. A correlation matrix Omega is positive semi-definite, and so its Cholesky factor L is not unique. Constraining one element of L to equal unity makes makes L identifiable, and so the (1,1)-entry of L is constrained to equal unity.

Question 2: Is this reasoning correct?

[I think this question is general enough to not require code, but if I am wrong, let me know and I will post something.]

messages.body_plain:
> On Apr 18, 2015, at 1:37 AM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Friday, April 17, 2015 at 10:51:03 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On Apr 18, 2015, at 12:39 AM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > On Friday, April 17, 2015 at 10:19:04 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> [snip]
> The posterior has to be proper or NUTS will run with the
> impropriety.
>
> I just meant in my response that an extra normal(0,1) variable
> will absolutely not kill the NUTS condition and not slow things
> down overall very much.
>
> I was not disagreeing, sorry if that wasn't clear.
>
>
>
> > I recall there's some parameter that limits the maximum number of steps but not what it's called.
>
> That just masks the problem.  Whenver you bump up against the limit, either
> the model needs to be fixed or the limit needs to be extended.  It's there
> so Stan doesn't just hang on the first go-round.
>
> >  If the prior is normal(0,sigma) (i.e. the parameter is an unused random effect level) you could get the funnel posterior and have a similar problem, but only if sigma is estimated to be large...  and that's where my intuition for this runs out.
>
> This isn't relevant if you have a fixed normal(0,1) prior,
> or even if it's a hierarchical prior that's well constrained.
>
> The problem with the funnel is the curvature issue --- with
> high hyperprior variance, the posterior is flat, whereas with
> low hyperprior variance, the posterior is very sharply curved.
> So you can't get a mass matrix and step-size that work everywhere.

By well constrained, I meant the hierarchical parameters, so that
you really get the effect of sampling from a fixed normal.

Which brings us to your next paragraph :-)

> I was just coming up with other situations where you could loose efficiency and if you have a hierarchical model where sigma is large (e.g.-outliers, but mostly well-estimated) then an unused random effect would have the funnel posterior and if the mass matrix gets estimated wrong (small step size) then it would kill performance when sigma got large at later iterations.  I've had this happen for a mark-recapture model with per-occasion random effects for recapture, so I think it's worth being careful with weeding out parameters for batches with no/little data in a hierarchical model.

Absolutely.  That's one of the reasons we've been going toward
stronger priors and hyperpriors.

And if at all possible, unused parameters should be removed.  It
just makes everything less efficient.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi all!
I have performed some tests following your advices:
1. Try to set a smaller step and higher acceptance rate [see attempt 1 in R code epilepsy_model_ODE.R]--> FAIL
2. Try to set all the initial estimates at reasonable values ( and also at  "0")  [see attempt 2.1 and 2.2 in R code epilepsy_model_ODE.R]--> both FAIL
3. Try not to give an infusion of 1 hour but a bolus fixing the initial condition of the first compartment  [see attempt 3 in R code epilepsy_model_ODE.R]-->FAIL
4. Try to fix all the parameters at reasonable values and estimate only one parameter (for ex. I tried first Vmax and then Q)  [see  R code epilepsy_model_ODE_fix.R]-->FAIL

The priors (except for Vmax and KM1 are all already informative). Maybe I can use normal distributions rather than gamma distribution (even if gamma distribution for precisions is more or less the standard). So, the problem seems to be the intrinsic stiffness of the model, even if this surprises me because it is a very simple PK model.
If you  want to have another look at the codes, I attached here R and stan files.
I have really appreciate your support!

Best regards,

E

messages.body_plain:
I got the sign right, but forgot the log! There's an absolute value.
The Jacobian adjustment on the log scale adds

  log | d/du f(u) |

  = log | d/du u^(-1) |

  = log | - u^(-2) |

  = log | u^(-2) |

  = log ( u^(-2) )

  = -2 * log(abs(u))

so you want

  increment_log_prob(-2 * log(abs(u)));

That last abs() is to account for

  u^(-2) = (1 / u^2)

being positive by by construction.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Everybody,
 I have two positive_ordered random variables. While these make the model general, they lead to a problem of identifiability. I would like to artificially make them prefer smaller values when possible. How can I achieve this?

The problem I have is the following :

hf~lognormal(hf_mu,hf_sigma);
sf~lognormal(sf_mu,sf_sigma);

I would like sf>hf>0 and both sf and hf as close to zero as possible. How can I achieve this in a sensible way?
Thanks,
Sunil.

messages.subject: FITC GP approximation with Stan?
messages.subject_clean: FITC GP approximation with Stan?
messages.body_plain:
I have logistic spatial data with a linear (non-spatial) covariate, and would like to like to model it with a GP (with unknown scale). The number of data points is around 300–600, and a straightforward logistic GP model with Stan seems slow. (I have tried it, with reparameterizations, jitter, etc.).

Is there any reason why the FITC approximation would not be feasible with Stan?
The matrix computations seem slightly complicated, and my main worry is that gradients would not be that fast.

Any other recommendations? (I'm not very familiar with GP's.) I mainly care about the mean, so would something simpler be sufficient? Would GPstuff be able to do GP's with linear covariates?

On Sunday, April 19, 2015 at 7:00:59 PM UTC+3, Janne Sinkkonen wrote:
> I have logistic spatial data with a linear (non-spatial) covariate, and would like to like to model it with a GP (with unknown scale). The number of data points is around 300–600, and a straightforward logistic GP model with Stan seems slow. (I have tried it, with reparameterizations, jitter, etc.).
>
> Is there any reason why the FITC approximation would not be feasible with Stan?
> The matrix computations seem slightly complicated, and my main worry is that gradients would not be that fast.

For that data size the benefit of FITC is likely to be small unless number of inducing points is very small. Currently autodiff is likely to be slow. There is a project for improving GPs in Stan, but it's going to take some time...

>
> Any other recommendations? (I'm not very familiar with GP's.) I mainly care about the mean, so would something simpler be sufficient? Would GPstuff be able to do GP's with linear covariates?

GPstuff can handle linear covariates easily. It's likely that you could also get fast good results with EP instead of MCMC for latent values. You can email me if you want more help with GPstuff.

Aki

messages.body_plain:
It helps to have more context in a model here.  If hf and sf are
scalars, then you can declare the pair of them to be ordered and
positive as:

real<lower=0> hf;
real<lower=hf> sf;

This will guarantee sf > hf.  But it can distort the posterior if
it's not physically impossible to have mean(sf) > mean(hf) but
some draw m having nsf_m < hf_m.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Bob for the response. I will give you a little more context.

The generative process :

There are two entities:

A  and B

A private info : val_mu, val_sigma, hf, sf and sf>=hf>=0, random variable val~lognormal(val_mu,val_sigma)

B's goal is to estimate val_mu, val_sigma, hf and sf

B presents A  a value "bid" and
A draws a "val" from "lognormal(val_mu,val_sigma)"

if(val<bid and val>hf) {
  B wins the auction and has to pay price(called second bid (sb) ) as follows :
  if (bid>sf) {
    sb = max(val,sf)
  } else {
    sb = bid
  }
} else {
  B loses the bid.
}

The data is generated using the stan code in "second_bid_gen.stan" attached to this email.
from the data generated from the model, I am trying to infer the values of val_mu, val_sd, hf and sf from the generated data using the stan code in "second_bid_sf.stan".

following the example in your earlier solution, I split the data into winning and losing bids. On a losing bid, one only know his own bid (referred to as lb) . But on winning a bid, we have the value we bid (referred to as wb) and the price we have to pay, second bid (referred to as sb). I realized that the following relations hold for the above generative process.

if (wb==sb)
  sb~(pdf_of(max(val,hf))*p(sb<sf)+pdf_of(max(val,sf))*p(sb>sf)
else
  sb~pdf_of(max(val,sf))

The losing bid contributes the following term to the log-probability
log(1-cdf_of(max(hf,val))(lb) )

While I feel my above formulation is correct. I would love to hear if you find any discrepancy.

cdf_of(max(hf,val)) = cdf_hf(x)*cdf_val(x)
pdf_of(max(hf,val)) = d/dx (cdf_hf(x)*cdf_val(x)) = cdf_hf(x)*pdf_val(x) + pdf_hf(x)*cdf_val(x)

p(sb<sf) = 1-cdf_sf(sb)
p(sf<sb) = cdf_sf(sb)

While I feel most of what I have done above is correct, I am unable to come up with a reasonable
prior distributions for sf and hf. I would greatly appreciate any help/advice you may have.

Thanks a tonne in advance.

Sunil.

messages.body_plain:
The usual ESS estimators use just one chain — we use a slightly more
sophisticated estimators which considers multiple chains and is far
more sensitive to poor mixing (which is a good thing).  If you’ve
just run one then what happens is that we split the one chain into
two and use our multi-chain estimator.

Naively looking at your trace plot O(100) seems reasonable to me —
although there is high-frequency variation there is a slower low-frequency
component with a period on the order of 100 samples, and this should
drive the ESS calculation.  I’m guess the coda estimator is just not
sensitive enough to catch this lower-frequency component.

messages.body_plain:
RStan does round n_eff to the nearest integer with the following code

 s$summary[, 'n_eff'] <- round(s$summary[, 'n_eff'], 0)

> On Apr 21, 2015, at 12:28 PM, Jonah <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:

>
>  s$summary[, 'n_eff'] <- round(s$summary[, 'n_eff'], 0)

Neat.  I didn't realize it specialized by column (just n_eff it looks like).

I also didn't realize digits=1 was just digits after decimal
place, not arithmetic precision:

     mean se_mean   sd  2.5%  25%  50%  75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
x     0.0     0.0  1.0  -1.9 -0.7  0.0  0.7   1.9  3073    1

So digits=3 gives you the same 4 digits of precision on n_eff but increases
precision on mean to 2 digits and 97.5% interval to 4 digits.

       mean se_mean     sd    2.5%    25%    50%    75%  97.5% n_eff  Rhat
x     0.016   0.018  0.992  -1.885 -0.668  0.010  0.688  1.937  3073 1.000

Alas, the only alternative that lets you align columns is scientific notation,
and I believe Andrew already vetoed that in general.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to play with fitting a linear model with M-coefficients being drawn from a multi-normal prior (a dump version of the sample from manual) and N sets of observations

STAN code, R data and results are attached.

Four Questions:

Q1. During the fitting process, I noticed the engine through out a lot of rejection messages (mostly during warmup, but also occasionally during sampling)

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
stan::prob::lkj_corr_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): y is not positive definite. y(0,0) is 1:0
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

However:

a. Rhat seems ok, except one of the omega has NaN
b. the coefficient posterior seems reasonable resemble that from a simple multiple regression (the 2 coefficients are quite independent).

So, going back to the error messages:  Is that due to my model specification or lack of data or nothing to worry about?

Q2. This is a bit of generalization question: For a model with M-coefficients, what's the typical size needed for N (observation sizes)? In my problem domain, N is not large - in the order of 10s. I'm trying to get a sense of realistically, how many predictors I can use.

Q3. I tried to do the cholesky factorization (code attached: multi_norm_ch.stan) and the engine now spills out *a lot* of messages complaining beta being negative:

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
Invalid value of beta: validate transformed params(N4stan5agrad3varE): beta[2] is -3.27553:0, but must be greater than or equal to 0
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

I would guess the issue is that I have beta lower bounded at 0 and the computation in the transformed parameters can volatile that.

Question is: what should i do in the transformed parameter block to ensure lower bound is not violated?

Q4: I would like to use the model to do posterior prediction. In the generated quantities block, is following sufficient if I want to take in consideration of the covariance.

eal y_tilde;
y_tilde <- normal_rng (X_tilde * beta, sigma);
(assuming X_tilde is now supplied)

Many thanks,

Andy

> I had a go at this but it doesn't seem to have worked. I downloaded the stan source files from your github, and linked to the eigen and boost libraries when compiling my model using the Rstan function stan(), but I still get the tgamma errors when I run my model.

Unless you've rebuilt RStan from scratch, I would expect the interface to change just based on downloading the Stan source code from GitHub. The instructions that Bob posted were for compiling C++ directly from the command line. If you're trying to write custom C++, you'll have to start with the command line before trying to get it integrated through RStan. It can be done, it just requires more config and more steps.

>
> So instead I have been looking into coding up a log gamma cdf function in C++. I read on another mailing list post that any functions you use in C code has to be understood by autodiff. Does this mean I cannot use binary arithmetic, break statements and the like? Or are there functions that autodiff understands, but are not included in the stan manual?

The Stan C++ api has binary arithmetic, you can use break statements, and we've also reimplemented all of the standard math library, so that's all available, the documentation is a little light, but what we have is written in doxygen and if you don't have doxygen installed, grab a tagged version of the repository. It'll have the generated html webpages under doc/api.

There's also a wki page that describes the use of the autodiff library.

messages.body_plain:
> On Apr 21, 2015, at 9:22 PM, Christopher Steele <steele...@googlemail.com> wrote:
>
> I had a go at this but it doesn't seem to have worked. I downloaded the stan source files from your github, and linked to the eigen and boost libraries when compiling my model using the Rstan function stan(), but I still get the tgamma errors when I run my model.

I'm not sure what you were trying.  That function's just what gets called
in a Stan program.

>
> So instead I have been looking into coding up a log gamma cdf function in C++. I read on another mailing list post that any functions you use in C code has to be understood by autodiff. Does this mean I cannot use binary arithmetic, break statements and the like?

Break statements are fine.  By binary arithmetic, you mean bit fiddling like the
binary | and & or << and <<< shift operations?

The trick is that any functions or operations that are involved in the result
have to be auto-diffable.  So if you bit fiddle to do something like choose which
iterative algorithm to run, that'll probably be OK, but you'll have to be careful
in how you pull the bits out.

We're happy to advise if you have something specific in mind, like a stable
C++ algorithm that works on double values that you just want to translate to
something that can be autodiffed.

And it's no holds barred if you implement custom derivatives for the code.  I think
you'll find the problem is that there's not a very big range through which CDFs can
be autodiffed due to floating point representations themselves (that is, they don't
have enough range to represent the derivatives in many cases).

> Or are there functions that autodiff understands, but are not included in the stan manual?

Nope --- they're all in the manual.  But control's separate --- you can use
the regular loops, while, conditionals, etc., the ternary operator, etc.  You just
can't import a third-party library and use its functions.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Density functions on the normal scale
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Density functions on the normal scale
messages.body_plain:
Any hint as to why you need it on the linear scale?  You usually
want to keep everything on the log scale at all times because the
linear scale is so unstable for probability densities.

So no, there's no direct density functions built into the Stan
language.  You can implement poisson directly, but you'll find
it has

  poisson(y, lambda) = pow(lambda,y) * exp(-lambda) / gamma(y + 1)

But you very quickly run into overflow and underflow issues on
the linear scale if you do this directly rather than exponentiating
on the log scale (e.g., lambda better be < 750 or so or exp(-lambda)
will underflow to zero).

- Bob

messages.subject: multivariate probit R simulation and Stan model
messages.subject_clean: multivariate probit R simulation and Stan model
messages.body_plain:
I feel like a traveling salesman who at each stop is asked
to perform a new demonstration of Stan.  For today's demo,
Michael McCarthy, a quant ecologist in Melbourne wanted a
multivariate probit for some occupancy models they're working
on.  Ask and ye' shall receive.

I'm attaching an R simulation script and Stan model to
fit a multivariate probit:

  http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariate_probit_model

This is a model where each observation y[n] is a binary D-vector
of values and comes with a real-valued K-vector of predictors x[n].
The point is to model the correlation of the responses in the
binary values for each output.

The multivariate probit is not to be confused with multinomial
probit (where each observation y[n] is a single value in 1:K).

Getting the multivariate probit coded in Stan involves

  * the latent variable parameterization where each y[n,d] gets
    a parameter z[n,d]

  * declaring z[n,d] to have a lower bound of 0 if y[n,d] = 1 and
    an upper bound of 0 if y[n,d] = 0.

       - this involved the transformed data to split the y
         into positive and negative indexings

       - declaring separate y vectors with appropriate constraints

       - using transformed params to put them back togetehr

  * using a correlation matrix rather than covariance matrix to identify
    the scale (see the Wikipedia article for a 2D example)

       - then putting it on the Cholesky factor parameterization to
         allow both a prior and some degree of efficiency.

       - reconstructing the correlation matrix in the generated quantities block

It would also be possible to deal with unknown values of y or
new predictions.  For missing values of y, there'd be a third parallel
array of unconstrained vectors that'd go in the same way.  For predictions,
you'd want to do multi_normal RNGs in the generated quantities block and
threshold for efficiency.

- Bob

P.S.  Next step would be figuring out how to encapsulate some of that
      work in the .stan file into functions that could be reused.  It'll be
      crazy making to do this on a model-by-model basis.

messages.subject_clean: some general Stan advice
messages.body_plain:
Hi, see responses below.

> On Apr 21, 2015, at 3:56 AM, andy...@cubist-asia.com wrote:
>
> Hi all,
>
> I am trying to play with fitting a linear model with M-coefficients being drawn from a multi-normal prior (a dump version of the sample from manual) and N sets of observations
>
> STAN code, R data and results are attached.
>
> Four Questions:
>
> Q1. During the fitting process, I noticed the engine through out a lot of rejection messages (mostly during warmup, but also occasionally during sampling)
>
> Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
> stan::prob::lkj_corr_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): y is not positive definite. y(0,0) is 1:0
> If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
> but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

This is ok but it is worth looking back at the model to make sure it makes sense.  We recommend the usual steps:

- Build up your final model, starting with something smaller that you understand well, then adding features one by one and digesting each step.  We call this the network of models.

- Fake-data checking, where you simulate data from the model and then fit the model to the data and check that you can (approximately) recover the original parameters.  We have a vision of implementing this semi-automatically using a graphical model wrapper in R/Python/Julia/etc but we’re not there yet.

>
> However:
>
> a. Rhat seems ok, except one of the omega has NaN

Nan isn’t good; you should check that!

> b. the coefficient posterior seems reasonable resemble that from a simple multiple regression (the 2 coefficients are quite independent).
>
> So, going back to the error messages:  Is that due to my model specification or lack of data or nothing to worry about?
>
> Q2. This is a bit of generalization question: For a model with M-coefficients, what's the typical size needed for N (observation sizes)? In my problem domain, N is not large - in the order of 10s. I’m trying to get a sense of realistically, how many predictors I can use.

The larger M, the stronger a prior you’ll need.  We’ve been moving toward routinely using informative priors (my current favorite is to give everything N(0,1) on the unconstrained scale by default, assuming that the model has been scaled so that parameters are roughly of order 1 (so, for example, in a regression, you want your predictors to be of order 1, nothing like .000324 or 7383249).

> Q3. I tried to do the cholesky factorization (code attached: multi_norm_ch.stan) and the engine now spills out *a lot* of messages complaining beta being negative:
>
> Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
> Invalid value of beta: validate transformed params(N4stan5agrad3varE): beta[2] is -3.27553:0, but must be greater than or equal to 0
> If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
> but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.
>
> I would guess the issue is that I have beta lower bounded at 0 and the computation in the transformed parameters can volatile that.
>
> Question is: what should i do in the transformed parameter block to ensure lower bound is not violated?

In general I think it’s a bad idea to bound parameters like this.  If a parameter has a natural bound, sure (for example, scale parameters must be positive, probabilities must be between 0 and 1, correlations must be between -1 and 1, etc).  But if you just want a coefficient to be positive, don’t use a hard bound; instead use a soft constraint, e.g. a N(1,1) prior.

> Q4: I would like to use the model to do posterior prediction. In the generated quantities block, is following sufficient if I want to take in consideration of the covariance.
>

> real y_tilde;

> y_tilde <- normal_rng (X_tilde * beta, sigma);
> (assuming X_tilde is now supplied)

Yes, it’s that simple!

messages.body_plain:
hi,
it looks as if you are trying to implement prospect theory for gambles with only positive, only negative, and mixed gambles.
A way to start with a simpler model would be to start with one type of  gambles, get this working, and then ad more gamble types.

You could also use different constraints and priors for your parameters. in particular, I don't think all the parameters you have constrained to be below 1 need to or even should be constrained like that. a lower bound of 0 should suffice. (and a more informative prior than uniform(0,1) would be helpful).

it also looks as if you are using the softmax choice rule (which was also popularized by Duncan Luce for modeling decision making). if I remember correctly, stan has a softmax function. regardless if you use this or your one softmax, it is important to remember that the effect of your luce parameter depends on the scale of the outcomes of your gambles (i.e. do your outcomes vary between -5 and 5 or between -1000 and 1000). Therefore, the prior for the luce parameter should be chosen depending on the scale of your payoffs.

cheers-guido

messages.subject_clean: more efficient way to write PPCA model?
messages.body_plain:
It's possible to analytically integrate out either:

a) x, as was done in the original article by Tipping & Bishop (see section 3.1 http://research.microsoft.com/pubs/67218/bishop-ppca-jrss.pdf)
b) A, see article: Probabilistic Non-linear Principal Component Analysis with
Gaussian Process Latent Variable Models by Neil Lawrence (link: http://jmlr.org/papers/volume6/lawrence05a/lawrence05a.pdf)

Both will give simple mv-Gaussian likelihood with certain mean&covariance matrix. By doing option b), we can easily see that PCA correspond to Gaussian process with linear covariance function (and by changing the covariance function we can get non-linear dimension reduction models etc)

Thanks for sharing!  I love these knitr docs that include
everything for a model from simulation to fit.  It's the format
I'd like to adopt for all of our examples (at least those done
in R --- IPython Notebooks would do the same work).

Identification's  a tricky business.  Presumably Doug Rivers
was talking about MLE identification in his 2003 paper.
I'm not sure how your parameterization in terms of a product
minus a sum is identifiable --- it always hurts my head to
think about these.

We'd have made your life a lot easier if we had a lower-triangular
data type or even general ragged matrices!

That knitr-HTML-rendered LaTeX could use some work in spacing,
like between probablity terms in multiplications.

I didn't understand the hex plot.  Why are there hexagons and
why are they all touching?

The print output's still too much to scan in a presentation, but
it's nice to see it so users know what to do if they follow your example.
I'm always torn about that, because a visualization of the means (and
perhaps uncertainties) would be easier to scan --- maybe even scatterplots
of the two alpha components.

The person order vs. number of correct responses is hard to
understand --- wouldn't a histogram have been easier?

- Bob

On Wednesday, April 22, 2015 at 11:34:36 AM UTC+8, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hi, see responses below.
>
> > On Apr 21, 2015, at 3:56 AM, andy...@cubist-asia.com wrote:
> >
> > Hi all,
> >
> > I am trying to play with fitting a linear model with M-coefficients being drawn from a multi-normal prior (a dump version of the sample from manual) and N sets of observations
> >
> > STAN code, R data and results are attached.
> >
> > Four Questions:
> >
> > Q1. During the fitting process, I noticed the engine through out a lot of rejection messages (mostly during warmup, but also occasionally during sampling)
> >
> > Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
> > stan::prob::lkj_corr_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): y is not positive definite. y(0,0) is 1:0
> > If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
> > but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.
>
> This is ok but it is worth looking back at the model to make sure it makes sense.  We recommend the usual steps:
>
> - Build up your final model, starting with something smaller that you understand well, then adding features one by one and digesting each step.  We call this the network of models.
>
> - Fake-data checking, where you simulate data from the model and then fit the model to the data and check that you can (approximately) recover the original parameters.  We have a vision of implementing this semi-automatically using a graphical model wrapper in R/Python/Julia/etc but we’re not there yet.
>
> >
> > However:
> >
> > a. Rhat seems ok, except one of the omega has NaN
>
> Nan isn’t good; you should check that!
>
> > b. the coefficient posterior seems reasonable resemble that from a simple multiple regression (the 2 coefficients are quite independent).
> >
> > So, going back to the error messages:  Is that due to my model specification or lack of data or nothing to worry about?
> >
> > Q2. This is a bit of generalization question: For a model with M-coefficients, what's the typical size needed for N (observation sizes)? In my problem domain, N is not large - in the order of 10s. I’m trying to get a sense of realistically, how many predictors I can use.
>
> The larger M, the stronger a prior you’ll need.  We’ve been moving toward routinely using informative priors (my current favorite is to give everything N(0,1) on the unconstrained scale by default, assuming that the model has been scaled so that parameters are roughly of order 1 (so, for example, in a regression, you want your predictors to be of order 1, nothing like .000324 or 7383249).
>
> > Q3. I tried to do the cholesky factorization (code attached: multi_norm_ch.stan) and the engine now spills out *a lot* of messages complaining beta being negative:
> >
> > Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
> > Invalid value of beta: validate transformed params(N4stan5agrad3varE): beta[2] is -3.27553:0, but must be greater than or equal to 0
> > If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
> > but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.
> >
> > I would guess the issue is that I have beta lower bounded at 0 and the computation in the transformed parameters can volatile that.
> >
> > Question is: what should i do in the transformed parameter block to ensure lower bound is not violated?
>
> In general I think it’s a bad idea to bound parameters like this.  If a parameter has a natural bound, sure (for example, scale parameters must be positive, probabilities must be between 0 and 1, correlations must be between -1 and 1, etc).  But if you just want a coefficient to be positive, don’t use a hard bound; instead use a soft constraint, e.g. a N(1,1) prior.
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi, I don’t know enough about your model to say, but there are different sorts of theoretical constraints.  Sometimes you have a true constraint, for example you have a model E(y) = exp(-a*x), and x can be arbitrarily large, so “a” must be positive.  Other times it’s not a true constraint, for example you have an econ model with an elatisticity parameter and for theroetical reasons you think it must be postive.  Here I think it’s better not to put in a hard constraint but instead to let the data speak.
A

messages.body_plain:
If we were able to specify a vector lower bound in stan, we would have

 t_censored[n] ~ weibull(r, exp(-beta[group_censored[n]] / r));

where t_censored are parameters and are defined as

real<lower=censor_time> t_censored.

But we cannot do the above, so a t2_censored is defined with lower bound 1.  Essentially,
t2_censored = t_censored / censor_time

Then the distribution of t2_censored needs to be derived from the distribution of t_censored and that is why the second argument of the weibull distribution is divided by censor_time.

Jiqiang

It might help to put a prior on sigma (you can do it directly
or by putting a prior on sigma^2 and transforming).  You'd have
to see if too large sigma was causing problems.

Otherwise, you have to look and see what's correlated or not
fitting well and try to adjust priors, etc.

There are two big optimizations for what you're doing.

First, you want to use a Cholesky-factor parameterization of
the prior --- there's a description in the manual chapter on
regression in a section called something like "multivariate priors".

Second, it would be much more efficient to pull this out of the loop

>     increment_log_prob(normal_log(y[n], eta[n,1]+eta[n,2]*x+eta[n,3]*q,sigma_y));

and write this outside the loop:

  y ~ normal(col(eta,1) + col(eta,2) * x + col(eta,3) * q, sigma_y);

Hi - it's indeed an elasticity parameter of an econ model, such that I would have expected either:

a) the dependent variable to co-move with the predictors (i.e. +ve value)
b) the dependent variable cannot explain by the predictors (i.e. 0)

Furthermore, the size of our data set is rather constrained - teens at best, quite often, upper single digit and can contain outliers, either due to typo in data collection (i.e. the outlier shouldn't be there) or other situational idiosyncratic issues (i.e. the outlier should be there).

We are quite new to STAN and Bayesian. In the past, I have used simple OLS tools and found that these issues could  cause the engine to come up with -ve elasticity parameters. Hence, I have adopted the lower bound at 0. What would have been a more "native" Bayesian to handle this (or, it wouldn't really be an issue with Bayesian/STAN since the posterior would have captured this)?

Andy

messages.body_plain:
Hi, I’d suggest an informative prior, for example if you think the elasticity should be between 0 and 1, you could use a normal prior with mean 0.5 and sd 0.5.  The point is that you’d like to let the data speak but at the same time you want to control your estimate.  If you do get a negative elasticity estimate, so be it (sometimes such things can happen due to unforeseen interactions in the data) but then you’ll probably also have a big standard error.  And if the data really “want” to find a negative elasticity with a small s.e., you’d like to know this—as, at the very least, this will tell you that there’s something weird about the data.  Better to let the data speak than to get an estimate right on the boundary which still doesn’t fit the data.

A

Note to Bob:  We should throw this advice into whatever file we’re keeping with general advice, so we can throw it into the forthcoming book!

What would have been a more "native" Bayesian to handle this (or, it wouldn't really be an issue with Bayesian/STAN since the posterior would have captured this)?

If you have outliers in the data due to data collection, then
you either want to move to a full measurement-error model where
you model the errors, or you can hack it in the existing model
by making a more robust noise model (such as a Student-t of low
degrees of freedom).

You can also add penalties for OLS --- Stan also has a penalized maximum
likelihood estimator.

- Bob

bias to the axes like a square tiling does (in a square tiling
diagonal moves are awkward and so the eye tends to follow
horizontal and vertical lines).  In practice that’s way more

and I’ve never found it particularly compelling as a
visualization argument.  If the appearance of the plot is that
sensitive to the tiling then make the tiles smaller, and if you
can’t make them any smaller than you don’t really have enough
data yield a reasonable histogram estimator of the density.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] more efficient way to write PPCA model?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] more efficient way to write PPCA model?
messages.body_plain:
You can integrate out parameters in Stan, too.  In fact,
you have to for discrete parameters.  You just need to
write down the appropriate density from which you want to sample.
You can then use the expectations of the parameters, which is
typically all you need for inference.

The bonus is that integrating out some of the parameters
almost always makes things faster (computing expectations
is almost always more efficient both computationally and
statistically than sampling --- it's the Rao-Blackwell theorem
in action).

- Bob

What do you need it for?  The generated quantities block has a categorical_rng.

There's no way to sample discrete parameters (other than hacks we don't
recommend) in the model.

If you need the parameters for inference, you want to marginalize
them out.

I don't know what you mean by belonging to the set {100, 200, 500}.
Our categorical outcomes are always 1:K for some K.  If you need
other numbers, you'll have to multiply or map them back again, say
using an array:

  int values[3];
  values[1] <- 100;
  values[2] <- 200;
  values[3] <- 500;

  c <- categorical_rng(rep_vector(1.0 / 3.0, 3));
  r <- values[c];
