messages.body_plain:
I'm reposting this in the hope that someone reading the RStan
issue tracker will help.  But this isn't the place to ask
questions --- it's for bugs or feature requests.  Discussions should
start on the users list, so I'm cc-ing that.

You can use Stan's own L-BFGS optimizer.  And we've found that
in some cases it's better to not transform a constrained parameter, but
just define it as:

  real sigma;

rather than

  real<lower=0> sigma;

There's no programmatic way to turn the constraints off.  You can turn
the Jacobian off for the adjustment, which you want to do if you're
trying to fit an MLE.  It's an argument in the log_prob method on a fit
object.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi, I have a new question related to the same shifted log normal hierarchical model.

The problem that I had at the beginning was that I was modeling the distribution of rt (reading times) like this:

(rt-c) ~ lognormal(log_mu, sigma);

and in some cases rt-c <0

where
c[i] <-  shift + shift_u[subj[i]];

and both shift and shift_u are parameters, shift is the general shift and shift_u is the shift that each subject has

so you (Bob C.) explained that I should constrain the shift to prevent rt-c <0
and I also constrained shift so that c is positive:

      real<lower=shift_bounds(shift_u,subj,rt)[1],
           upper=shift_bounds(shift_u,subj,rt)[2]> shift;

with a function:
functions {
 vector shift_bounds(row_vector shift_u, int[] subj, vector rt) {

     vector[2] shift_bounds;
    real shift_min;
    real shift_max;
    shift_min <- negative_infinity();

    shift_max <- positive_infinity();
    for (i in 1:num_elements(rt)){

         shift_min <- fmax(shift_min, - shift_u[subj[i]] );
         shift_max <- fmin(shift_max,rt[i] - shift_u[subj[i]] );

        }
    shift_bounds[1] <- shift_min;
    shift_bounds[2] <- shift_max;

    return shift_bounds;
  }
}

 So far so good. It worked pretty well.

Now the issue is what happens if shift_u isn't a part of the  parameters section but of transformed parameters. I assume that the individual shift may be correlated with the by subject intercept or slopes of the mean (the so-called random effects in linear mixed models). And then if I generate the shift_u from the same multivariate distribution that I use to generate the "random effects", how can I constrain the shift? I can't put it in parameters any longer because it depends on a transformed parameter, and if it's in transformed parameters it  should depend on another parameter.... So is there a the solution?
I hope I'm expressing myself clearly enough. And I might be doing something that doesn't make sense, in that case I'll be also happy to know it :)

I'm attaching the  latest version of the model (not working now).

Thanks!
Bruno

messages.body_plain:
The simple answer is "no" --- we can't use a sample as a prior.

Your best estimate for theta[i] is what it is with data items y[1], ..., y[i],
but when you see y[i+1], you don't want to freeze theta[1], ..., theta[i] --- that's the
cut behavior of BUGS.  Rather, you want to estimate them jointly given all
the data y[1], ..., y[i+1].

What do you mean by "real time"?  If you're looking at something with millisecond
responsiveness, I doubt Stan's going to be the right tool no matter what you do.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Like Andrew said — continued updating is problematic with MCMC because
samples do not a distribution make.  The go-to algorithm these days is
Sequential Monte Carlo, which is usually implemented with particles a la
particle filtering (the particle updates could be implemented with Adiabatic
Monte Carlo if the updating is particularly onerous).  You could use parts
of the Stan API to implement SMC but such an algorithm wouldn’t be in
Stan for a long time, if ever, as there are lots of complications to the
algorithm that prevent automated implementations.

Also, in my experience trying to approximate the posterior with a normal
(even a multivariate normal) rarely works for models with any nontrivial
structure.

Stochastic VB uses streaming data to estimate parameters that define
an approximating density (usually a normal).  It’s more robust than using
the empirical means/covariance to define a normal after each update,
but can still be tricky to implement for a general model.

messages.subject: Indexing a lookup table in Stan
messages.subject_clean: Indexing a lookup table in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan users,

Short question: does Stan have a function to return the index corresponding to the minimum value of a vector (i.e. argmin / which.min)? It doesn't appear to from the manual. If not, can anyone suggest a workaround for this? There is a thread with similar overtones here <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/find$20index$20of$20max$20value/stan-users/LK0kGNdyGdE/GJfWP5WCiyUJ> but it doesn't appear to offer the solution I'm looking for.

Background: My model contains a link function that is costly to compute. The link function takes an input value x and deterministically returns a new value y. The new value y doesn't depend on model parameters or data, only on x (which *does* depend on model parameters). Therefore, I thought would make sense to generate a lookup table of x and y values offline, pass this lookup table to Stan in the data block, and have Stan lookup y from its computed x value.

To do this in Python or R, I would subtract the (scalar) value of x from my lookup vector of x values (lookup_x), then use argmin / which.min to return the index of the lookup vector corresponding to the smallest absolute difference between x and lookup_x. I can then return y by indexing the lookup_y value corresponding to that index.

pseudocode:

diff = lookup_x - x
idx = argmin(abs(diff))
return lookup_y[idx]

Can anyone suggest how to do this in Stan?

Follow-up question: will using a lookup table in this fashion interfere with Stan's use of gradients? I could imagine that depending on the precision of my lookup table, I will need to turn down the tolerance on any gradient descent Stan is running. Suggestions or thoughts?

Thanks in advance,

Tom

messages.body_plain:
Ok, here's a first attempt using a loop (adapted from here <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/find$20index$20of$20max$20value/stan-users/LK0kGNdyGdE/GJfWP5WCiyUJ>). This defines a function in the function block:

    real lookup_fun(real x, int L, vector lookup_x, vector lookup_y){
        # return a y value from the lookup table corresponding to a given
        # x, lookup table vectors and the length of the lookup
        # table L.
        # assumes there is only one min.
        int min_idx;
        vector[L] diff;

        diff <- lookup_x - x;
        min_idx <- 1;

        for (i in 1:L){
            # absolute val only works for reals, not vector.
            diff[i] <- fabs(diff[i]);
            if (diff[i] < diff[min_idx]) {
                min_idx <- i;
            }

        # return corresponding y:
        return lookup_y[min_idx];
        }
    }

My model compiles and returns reasonable-looking values, but any advice on what problems I could be generating in the gradients by using a lookup table would be greatly appreciated.

Tom

messages.body_plain:
It’s not that the gradients are too coarse it’s that they don’t exist
(essentially the point where you map input -> index is discontinuous
and the discontinuity propagates through the rest of the gradient).

If this is a low-dimensional link function then I would consider
using a Gaussian process as a smooth, fast emulator, although
these can easily stray from the the true function after a few
dimensions so you have to be very vigilant.

all the transformed parameters satisfy whatever constraints you need.

messages.body_plain:
Ok, I found a good functional approximation to my link function, whose parameters I've hard-coded into the Stan model. This now converges beautifully.

Thanks for your help.

On Tuesday, April 28, 2015 at 3:47:49 PM UTC+2, Tom Wallis wrote:
> On Tuesday, April 28, 2015 at 3:38:59 PM UTC+2, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > It’s not that the gradients are too coarse it’s that they don’t exist
> > (essentially the point where you map input -> index is discontinuous
> > and the discontinuity propagates through the rest of the gradient).
>
> Ah huh. I was afraid of something like that.
>
> >
> > If this is a low-dimensional link function then I would consider
> > using a Gaussian process as a smooth, fast emulator, although
> > these can easily stray from the the true function after a few
> > dimensions so you have to be very vigilant.
>
> The link function is actually a simulation of discrete choices from a decision model with no analytic solution. However, the activity of the link function itself is only low dimensional (mapping x to y, and x is only ever a vector).
>
> Regarding your suggestion, I'm not sure I understand. Is that something that I would do in the body of my Stan model? In model 1, I would replace "lookup_fun" with "gp_pred" or similar? Or is the Gaussian process something that would be estimated outside Stan and then parameters passed to Stan somehow?
>
> >
> > On Apr 28, 2015, at 2:29 PM, Tom Wallis <tsaw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > > >
> > > > My model compiles and returns reasonable-looking values
> > >
> > > False. The values returned by the model never seem to move beyond the prior -- that is, somehow the parameters are not being updated.
> > >
> > > This seems to be that I'm using my (user-defined) functions incorrectly. In model_1.stan (attached), the model compiles and samples fine, but the parameter values never move away from the priors - like they're not being updated by the data. I guess this is a problem with me not understanding function scoping in Stan, because when I pull the code out of the functions and put it in the model block (see model_2.stan), this model seems to run.
> > >
> > > However, model_2.stan samples *extremely* slowly (as in, each iteration takes an extremely long time). I suspect this is because the gradients are too coarse, due to my lookup table. Does anyone have a suggestion as to how to improve this?
> > >
> > >
> > > >
> > > > On Tuesday, April 28, 2015 at 12:22:37 PM UTC+2, Tom Wallis wrote:
> > > > > Hi Stan users,
> > > > >
> > > > > Short question: does Stan have a function to return the index corresponding to the minimum value of a vector (i.e. argmin / which.min)? It doesn't appear to from the manual. If not, can anyone suggest a workaround for this? There is a thread with similar overtoneshere <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/find$20index$20of$20max$20value/stan-users/LK0kGNdyGdE/GJfWP5WCiyUJ> but it doesn't appear to offer the solution I'm looking for.
> > > > >
> > > > > Background: My model contains a link function that is costly to compute. The link function takes an input value x and deterministically returns a new value y. The new value y doesn't depend on model parameters or data, only on x (which *does* depend on model parameters). Therefore, I thought would make sense to generate a lookup table of x and y values offline, pass this lookup table to Stan in the data block, and have Stan lookup y from its computed x value.
> > > > >
> > > > > To do this in Python or R, I would subtract the (scalar) value of x from my lookup vector of x values (lookup_x), then use argmin / which.min to return the index of the lookup vector corresponding to the smallest absolute difference between x and lookup_x. I can then return y by indexing the lookup_y value corresponding to that index.
> > > > >

messages.body_plain:
If there’s a good function approximation that’s your best bet.

For posterity the GP would look something like

// put weakly informative priors on GP hyperparameters
// construct covariance matrix, Sigma, from training covariates
// add a gaussian process prior on the training data, y ~ normal(0, Sigma)
// use hyperparameters to construct predictive distribution for new y given new x
// use predictive y to model expensive function

You fit the GP to the training data and incorporate it into your
model at the same time, which maximizes the information.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Scope of variables declared in model block
messages.body_plain:
RStan has the ability to declare which parameters, transformed parameters,
and generated quantities go into the output.  CmdStan does not.  I
don't know about the other interfaces.

I'm guessing you'd like to see us

  * collapse the transformed parameters and model blocks into a single
    block,

  * allow variables declared at the top-level model block to be
    in-scope in generated quantities, and

  * add extra declarations (in language or out?) to control what goes
    into the output.

If not, could you provide a description and an example of what scope
behavior you'd like to see?

There has to be some interplay of scope and output.  For example,
it doesn't make sense to have nested local variables visible outside their
scopes, so I don't see how we could put them into the output.

There's also overhead in saving these things and passing them among
blocks --- the generated quantities have to retransform all the parameters
and reload all the transformed parameters into scope so they can be evaluated
with double values and not incur needless autodiff overhead.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bayesian Factor Analysis
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Bayesian Factor Analysis
messages.body_plain:
We also have a built-in function for you:

multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(L) = L * L'

when L is lower triangular.  We built it for just this purpose
and it'll be faster.

You also probably don't want to create the diagonal matrix
from psi

   Q <- L * L' + diag_matrix(psi);

just adding the values to the diagonal in a loop
would be faster.  I don't see a way to modify the Cholesky
factor easily to get the same effect --- that would be
even more efficient if it were possible.

- Bob

> On Apr 29, 2015, at 3:07 AM, Rick Farouni <rfar...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Mauricio,
>
> If you instead write  Q<-L*Phi*L'+diag_matrix(psi)  and add a sampling statement for Phi in the model block, then you can model  correlations among the factors. I'll do that for the next blog post. The factor analysis model I used  assumes that the factor scores are nuisance variables of no interest to the researcher. This can be the case in a confirmatory analysis  setting when the focus is on finding out which items (i.e. observed variables) are associated with which factor. If the focus on the other hand is on determining the latent factor scores (e.g. ability), then one would need  to incorporate the latent variables in the model, just as you did in the code you provided. The drawback is increased computation time.
>
> Rick,
>
>
> On Tuesday, April 28, 2015 at 12:34:14 PM UTC-4, Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal wrote:
> Hi Rick
>
> I see you use the covariance matrix method like SEM program (lavaan, Mplus). For Bayesian factor models I prefer to use the data model structure, estimating the factor scores, like Lee and Song (2012) recommend (http://www.amazon.com/Advanced-Bayesian-Structural-Equation-Modeling/dp/0470669527/ref=sr_1_2?ie=UTF8&qid=1430238405&sr=8-2&keywords=bayesian+structural+equation+modeling), this method is more flexible like making it easy to do interactions between factors.
>
> For example a model like that would be
>
> data{
> int N; // sample size
> int P; // number of variables
> int D; // number of dimensions
> vector[P] X[N]; // data matrix of order [N,P]
> }
>
> parameters{
> vector[P] b; // intercepts
> vector<lower=0>[P] lam; // factor loadings
> vector[D] FS[N]; // factor scores, matrix of order [N,D]
> corr_matrix[D] Rho; // correlation matrix between factors
> vector<lower=0>[P] var_p; // residual variance for each variable
> }
>
> transformed parameters{
> vector[D] M; // factor means
> vector<lower=0[D] Sd_d; // factor standard deviations
> vector[P] mu[N]; // predicted values
> matrix[D,D] Ld; // cholesky decomposition of the covariance matrix between factors
>
> for (m in 1:D) {
> M[m] <- 0;
> Sd_d[m] <- 1;}
>
> Ld <- diag_matrix(Sd_d) * cholesky_decompose(Rho);
>
> for(i in 1:N){
> mu[i,1] <- b[1] + lam[1]*FS[i,1];
> mu[i,2] <- b[2] + lam[2]*FS[i,1];
> mu[i,3] <- b[3] + lam[3]*FS[i,1];
> mu[i,4] <- b[4] + lam[4]*FS[i,2];
> mu[i,5] <- b[5] + lam[5]*FS[i,2];
> mu[i,6] <- b[6] + lam[6]*FS[i,2];
> mu[i,7] <- b[7] + lam[7]*FS[i,3];
> mu[i,8] <- b[8] + lam[8]*FS[i,3];
> mu[i,9] <- b[9] + lam[9]*FS[i,3];
> }
> }
>
> model{
>
> b ~ normal(0, 100);
> lam ~ normal(0.4,var_p);
> var_p ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
>
> for(i in 1:N){
> X[i] ~ normal(mu[i],var_p);
> FS[i] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(M, Ld);
> }
>
> }
>
>
> Bye
>
> - Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Scope of variables declared in model block
messages.body_plain:
On 2015-04-28 Tue 22:40, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> RStan has the ability to declare which parameters, transformed parameters,
> and generated quantities go into the output.  CmdStan does not.  I
> don't know about the other interfaces.
>
> I'm guessing you'd like to see us
>
>   * collapse the transformed parameters and model blocks into a single
>     block,
>
>   * allow variables declared at the top-level model block to be
>     in-scope in generated quantities, and
>
>   * add extra declarations (in language or out?) to control what goes
>     into the output.
>
> If not, could you provide a description and an example of what scope
> behavior you'd like to see?

I don’t have a specific proposal at this point, I’m still trying to
understand how these things work in Stan (but yes, I was considering the
points you list above).

There are two separate issues: what goes into the output and what is
visible in subsequent blocks (let’s ignore variables in nested
blocks).  However, there is no way to handle these issues
separately.  There is only one mechanism to control both and that is
putting variables into transformed parameters.  However, that is not
always desirable: I’m currently working on a model that has a loop in
the model block in which I do two things: transformation of parameters
and definition of priors for the parameters.  However, I also need
access to the transformed parameters in generated quantities.  To
achieve that, I have to move the transformation of the parameters to
transformed parameters.  That, however, means that I need two loops
instead of one – one in transformed parameters and one in the model
block for assignment of the priors – and that makes the model
slower.  The slowdown is probably also due to the overhead of passing
stuff from transformed parameters to the model block.

So it seems that I’m forced to implement the model in a less efficient
way just because transformed parameters is the only way to control the
visibility of variables.  Making the transformed parameters visible also
gives me the undesired side-effect that they clutter the output where I
don’t need them.

My solution was to do the transformation in the model block for speed
and to transform the parameters a second time in generated
quantities.  This is reasonably fast but makes the whole model
definition unnecessarily complex and error-prone.  It’s also not quiet
as efficient as it could be because of the redundant calculations.  I
don’t know how to address this but at the moment it feels like
Stan is making me jump through hoops.  Could be all my fault, though,
and perhaps there is an elegant solution that I’m simply not seeing.

> There has to be some interplay of scope and output.  For example,
> it doesn't make sense to have nested local variables visible outside their
> scopes, so I don't see how we could put them into the output.

Yes, I agree.  My concern is only about variables declared in non-nested
blocks.

  Titus

> There's also overhead in saving these things and passing them among
> blocks --- the generated quantities have to retransform all the parameters
> and reload all the transformed parameters into scope so they can be evaluated
> with double values and not incur needless autodiff overhead.

messages.body_plain:
I have some modeling code that I've been testing out, and in one of my test cases with synthetic data I get the error "Rejecting user-specified initialization because of divergent gradient."

This is the line of code that produces the error:

    fit <- rstan::sampling(sm, data=data, chains=1, warmup=1, iter=1, init=list(params), test_grad=TRUE)

When I subsequently call

    val <- rstan::log_prob(fit, rstan::unconstrain_pars(fit, params))

the value I get is reasonable (around -20000). When I repeatedly call rstan::log_prob to compute a finite-differences approximation to the gradient, using a delta of +/- 1e-4, all components of the gradient has absolute values less than 300.

This has me utterly confused. Can you get the "divergent gradient" error for any reason other than a very large gradient value?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bayesian Factor Analysis
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Bayesian Factor Analysis
messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, April 29, 2015 at 10:25:15 PM UTC-4, Rick Farouni wrote:
> Correct me if I am wrong but since Factor analysis is mainly a dimensionality reduction technique, the n x p  loading matrix L will have n larger than p, so the rank of L is at most p, (when L has full column rank) and the n x n matrix LL' would have the same rank of L and  so isn't positive definite. That is , if we consider L*L' as a covariance matrix, then it would be rank deficient and won't have a Cholesky factor.  As for A=B*C, I was referring to this rank decomposition  result <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore%E2%80%93Penrose_pseudoinverse#Rank_decomposition>.

If the reduced matrix is L * L', then its Cholesky factor is L conceptually. Nevertheless, Stan can't numerically distinguish between rank deficient and indefinite, so cholesky_decompose() would throw an exception.

BTW, if you are thinking of the model as EFA with the factors integrated out, you can use the likelihood that R uses:

> stats:::factanal.fit.mle
function (cmat, factors, start = NULL, lower = 0.005, control = NULL,
    ...)
{
    FAout <- function(Psi, S, q) {
        sc <- diag(1/sqrt(Psi))
        Sstar <- sc %*% S %*% sc
        E <- eigen(Sstar, symmetric = TRUE)
        L <- E$vectors[, 1L:q, drop = FALSE]
        load <- L %*% diag(sqrt(pmax(E$values[1L:q] - 1, 0)),
            q)
        diag(sqrt(Psi)) %*% load
    }
    FAfn <- function(Psi, S, q) {
        sc <- diag(1/sqrt(Psi))
        Sstar <- sc %*% S %*% sc
        E <- eigen(Sstar, symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)
        e <- E$values[-(1L:q)]
        e <- sum(log(e) - e) - q + nrow(S)
        -e
    }
...

That FAfn() function returns the log likelihood so you can express priors on the uniquenesses and not worry about the unidentified loadings. However, it assumes S is a correlation matrix, which makes more sense when doing maximum likelihood (which is invariant) than MCMC.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
This is a problem with the negative binomial CDF implementation.
Essentially the gradient requires some crazy hypergeometric
function derivatives that are all implemented with power series.
The initial implementation was not robust to large values and
would never converge.  We added a max iteration threshold,
but then the series just terminate prematurely and the resulting
gradients are inaccurate and cause the integrator to diverge.

Coincidentally enough, I encountered the same problem in
a model on which I’m working and spent way too much work
to fix it.  It’s currently under a pull request at
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/pull/1433.  It may still be
unstable for super pathological arguments, but it should be
much more robust.

You need to supply a positive argument to negative_binomial()
or negative_binomial_log().
